articles.title: The 15 Best Slasher Movies of All Time
articles.summary: Iconic slasher movies everyone should see at least once.
articles.body:
Movies have been scaring the wits out of folks for a century now and one of cinema's most effective terror delivery systems is the "slasher."

Yes, horror movies have dozens of sub-genres and one of horror's most sinister and enduring offshoots involves people scrambling for their lives while being stalked by a cunning, patient maniac. Inventive, gruesome deaths, a brutalized lone survivor, and the effortless promise of seemingly endless sequels, the slasher pits humans against themselves in a nasty fight to live through the night.

Sure, these killers sometimes have a supernatural advantage — whether they're undead, invading your dreams, or...you know, a pint-size doll. But most slasher psychos are just deranged murderers out to rack up record body counts, distinguishable usually only by their weapon and mask of choice.

The early '80s was a boom for slashers, which moved and morphed from pivotal pictures from horror masters to a glut of cheap knockoffs and copycats. By the end of 1984, the slasher “heyday" was kaput, but that didn't mean the slasher died off. No, like the killers in these movies, the slasher never truly dies. It's still one of the most dependable and diabolical branches of horror. Below you'll find the very best slashers ever made, some featuring the biggest horror villains of all time — like Jason Voorhees, Michael Myers, Chucky, and more!

Here are the 15 best slasher movies of all time.

Though there are some important slasher heavy-hitters that arrived before John Carpenter's Halloween (and you'll see them on this list, as well), nothing changed the game like Michael Myers' first outing as "The Shape."

Halloween — with its indie movie low budget, masterful score (also by Carpenter), and direct no-frills story — launched a thousand slow-moving madmen, turning the six years that followed it into SlasherMania. It even fell victim to its own influence as eventual sequels were mostly cheap cash-grabs, never matching the magic that Carpenter was able to achieve with the original.

Halloween a simple, scary campfire tale about a lunatic who escapes an asylum and returns to his hometown, stalking a teen girl and a young boy simply because they made the mistake of stopping by his childhood porch (sequels would give "meaning" to his target, and even to Michael's "evil"). Star Jamie Lee Curtis became an instant Scream Queen and earned an eternal place on the Final Girl Mount Rushmore. You can check out our explainer of the full Halloween timeline for more info about the other movies.

More Like This (worth seeing): Halloween II (1981), Halloween 4: The Return of Michael Myers (1988), Halloween H20 (1998), Halloween (2018)

Before Halloween there were a handful of standout slashers. Texas Chainsaw Massacre is one of the most aggressively terrifying movies ever made.

Sure, it struggled when it came to sequels (though the 2003 reboot was solid) as the premise itself, of a nasty cannibalistic family, was a tricky one to franchise (it also wouldn't get a single follow-up for 12 years) but like most first movies in a long-running horror franchise, it's the best. And it's complete. There's no actual need for more.

Tobe Hooper's mean, dirty road trip-gone-violently wrong touched on the changes happening to America at the time and the diminished role of farmers all while serving up an unsuspected group of young adults to a crazed, murderous family of outcasts. Leatherface, in particular, remains as a ghastly fixture of horror to this day, as a hulking, skin-wearing brute capable of killing folks with his bare hands...much less the chainsaw he wields with a butcher's precision.

The idea for Friday the 13th may have come about in a copycat manner, as the creators looked to replicate the success of Halloween by pairing a killer with a "notable day/holiday" but the film is very different from Halloween, playing out more in a "whodunnit?" fashion. Plus, it's massively influential in its own right.

Yes, some could even argue that Friday the 13th's success, while taking cues from Halloween, is the true start of the '80s maniac madness. And it turned the quaint, fun idea of summer camp into a go-to location for horror movies forever. Counselors would never know peace again, constantly placed in mortal peril thanks to the massacre at Camp Crystal Lake at the hands of a murderer out for righteous, misplaced revenge. It's a must-watch horror classic that helped set the template for slasher mysteries and twist killer reveals for years to come.

See our guide to the Friday the 13th movies in order for the full timeline.

By the mid-'80s, the slasher well was running a bit dry, carving the path for more bigger imaginations, wilder ideas, and new spins "unstoppable" killers. This is where the Nightmare on Elm Street movies began.

Wes Craven, who had already made a name for himself with '70s exploitation horror flicks The Last House on the Left and The Hills Have Eyes, created an instant-classic maniac in the form of already dead child murderer Freddy Krueger, who now, from beyond the grave, could attack and kill his victims in their dreams (which also had control over). A Nightmare on Elm Street is a legendary film, delivering terror in ways audiences had never seen before. Freddy himself became a pop-culture sensation (and eventually even a wise-cracking anti-hero in his own films) while Heather Langencamp's Nancy helped level up the Final Girl as she purposefully put herself on a collision course with Freddy in her own mind, and kicking his ass.

More Like This (worth seeing): A Nightmare on Elm Street 3: Dream Warriors (1987), A Nightmare on Elm Street 4: The Dream Master (1988), Wes Craven's New Nightmare (1994), Freddy vs. Jason (2003)

Setting Clive Barker's short story "The Forbidden" in Chicago's Cabrini–Green housing project was a master stroke of taking source material and breathing more meaningful life into it. Candyman is a tragedy, a love story, a slice of social commentary, and a movie where a lot of folks meet their end via a gross crusty hook all rolled into one. Tony Todd's seductive, almost Dracula-like killer, who haunts Cabrini–Green as a vengeful boogeyman, is an iconic monster born of America's violent racist past, now serving as a reminder that bigotry is still a solid fixture in our society. Candyman casts a huge, illustrious shadow in the somewhat horror-starved '90s, mixing supernatural chills with urban legend thrills.

More Like This (worth watching): Horror Noire: A History of Black Horror (2019), Candyman (2021)

Once again, by the back half of the '80s, regular human mass murderers were out and killers with crazy, cool powers were in. Freddy Krueger was ambushing teens in their dreams, Jason Voorhees was now a full-fledged zombie brought back from the dead, Michael Myers was part of some demonic cult, and... Lakeshore Strangler Charles Lee Ray found his soul trapped inside a "I'm your friend to the end" Good Guy doll, allowing him to continue terrify people as toy. Child's Play is miraculous for several reasons. Firstly, it works. Really well. It's an awesome movie. Secondly, Child's Play's decades of sequels, and recent ongoing TV series, are all part of the same timeline and continuity. And all written (and sometimes directed) by creator Don Mancini. That's unheard of in horror. Lastly, the Chucky brand is groundbreaking, over the last 30+ years, for LGBTQ+ representation and allyship. And all of this traces back to a tremendously fun and fiendish film about a poor young boy being blamed for the murderous actions of his doll. You can check out the full Child's Play timeline , which actually includes a TV series as well.

More Like This (worth watching): Child's Play 2 (1990), Bride of Chucky (1998), Chucky: The Series (2021- )

Wes Craven's Scream brought the quasi-dormant slasher genre back in a big way thanks to his masterful hand at suspenseful directing, a young charismatic cast, and a crackerjack meta-humor script from Kevin Williamson. It was a horror movie filled with characters raised on horror movies, and a mystery killer psychotically influenced by them. The Scream franchise is still going strong today thanks to the saga's ongoing "whodunnit?" premise, in which anyone could be the stab-happy Ghostface. The story's legacy characters, including Neve Campbell's stalwart surviving Final Girl Sidney Prescott, is another big draw, though the recent hit Scream movies have demonstrated that the bones of the story are strong enough to pass the torch to a new crew of young stars. Scream, despite being rooted in a love for '80s slashers, is timeless in a way. It speaks to the horror fan in all of us.

You can check our guide on where to watch the Scream movies for streaming details.

More Like This (worth watching): I Know What You Did Last Summer (1997), Urban Legend (1998), and any Scream movie

It's important to note that slashers were not purely an American pop-culture sensation, and that Italian horror master Dario Argento had been serving up spectacular slaughter all through the '70s, including many notable slashers. The best of his catalog, from a slasher standpoint, is Tenebrae, about an American author (Anthony Franciosa) on an international book tour who discovers that a serial killer has been inspired by his murder-mystery novel. Seen as Argento's masterwork of his favorite thriller genre, giallo (psychological/exploitation slasher), Tenebrae explores the nature of voyeurism, dark doubles, trauma, and death.

More Like This (worth watching): Blood and Black Lace (1964), The Bird with the Crystal Plumage (1970), Deep Red (1075), Opera (1987)

Friday the 13th: The Final Chapter (1984)

Okay, so why are there TWO Friday the 13th films on the list? Well, it's because of the huge (killer) shift between the first and second movie, with the latter introducing the character of Jason Voorhees. By the fourth Friday the 13th movie, Jason had taken over the series fully as the masked killer in the woods (permanently donning a hockey mask thanks to the third movie). Of the many Jason-filled sequels, Part 4, The Final Chapter , is the crowning achievement as it really was, at the time, designed to be Jason's final romp. Pure and simple, this film is epitome of everything the slasher genre had been built toward for years, complete with a killer who'd been up until now, unbeatable. While on a brand new murder spree, picking off a gaggle of young, horny cabin renters, Jason would ultimately meet his nemesis in young Tommy Jarvis (Corey Feldman), a boy whose quick thinking and savage machete skills would spell the (temporary) end for Mr. Voorhees.

More Like This (worth watching): Friday the 13th Part 2 (1981), Friday the 13th Part VI: Jason Lives (1986), Freddy vs. Jason (2003)

A cut above most slasher clones, The Burning is summer camp carnage at the hands of a previous caretaker horribly disfigured thanks to a prank gone wrong. Setting aside Friday the 13th similarities, The Burning makes its own distinct mark with suspense, gore, and nastiness. Directed by a Brit whose bread and butter were usually rock documentaries, and scored by prog rock icon Rick Wakeman, The Burning is largely considered one of the best of the era, for an era overflowing with lackluster and derivative horror. It has red in its ledger but its the perfect combination of camp (location), camp (tone), and actual scares.

Another surprising standout amongst the '80s slasher rabble is Slumber Party Massacre, one of the rare teen in terrifying turmoil movies directed by a woman, Amy Holden Jones (who would write Indecent Proposal and create Fox's The Resident... whaaaat?). Here, a madman on the loose, with a giant power drill, targets a suburban sleepover, but this film, even so early in '80s slasher boom, toys with horror conventions. Written as a parody, but filmed like a drama, Slumber Party Massacre flipped gender cliches on their head, giving us a group of proactive female characters who supported one another, and shirking the traditional gory deaths that usually befell women in these movies. Sometimes seen as a precursor to Scream, because of its "straightforward meets satire" sensibilities, this killer flick is definitely one to catch.

You might be asking: are there any more recent slasher offerings worth checking out? Absolutely. Happy Death Day (and it's even more bonkers sequel) provides a much-needed jolt to the aging genre, trapping its shallow narcissistic heroine, Tree (Jessica Rothe), in a time loop where she's killed over and over again on her birthday by the same masked killer. It's a sci-fi slasher-mystery that has Tree growing as a person while dying as a victim, all while trying to solve her own murder and unmask the culprit before she eventually dies too many times to keep looping. Rothe herself shines here in this miraculous combo of rom-com, college caper, and horror mystery. It also works as one of the best time-loop movies .

One classic slasher that never seems to get enough love is Black Christmas , an absolutely essential horror watch. Directed by Bob Clark — who would, yes, go on to direct 1983's A Christmas Story — Black Christmas is heralded by many as the first true North American slasher, in the genre's fullest form (mysterious killer looming, picking off teens/young adults via various methods). Based on an urban legend/campfire story commonly known as “The Babysitter and The Man Upstairs" (which would influence many horror movies, in general), the movie is set in a sorority house during the holidays, as a crazed killer, with no explained backstory, holes up in the house, hidden away, and murders his way through college students. Delivering genuine shock and suspense, Black Christmas is perpetually listed as one of the tip top slashers of all time.

If we're truly looking for the source code for all slashers, including the movie that influenced Halloween the most (just look at Halloween's opening sequence) it's Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho , which had unsuspecting '60s moviegoers full on fainting in theaters. Which an apex achievement for a horror movie (other winners include The Exorcist, Terrifier 2, etc). Purposefully filmed in black and white, Psycho was "Master of Suspense" Hitchcock's honest, earnest experiment in terror, unleashing a landmark murder scene so intense that it scarred a generation. The story of a woman on the run (Janet Leigh) seeking refuge in a motel run by the biggest "mama's boy" of all time (Anthony Perkins) pushed the horror genre forward by light years, inspiring an entire wave of new horror masters. It's also one of the best thriller movies of all time .

Okay look, Terrifier is unhinged, absurdly gory ugliness. Perhaps made even more unsettling by its ultra-small budget (though the makeup effects do not skimp). We're providing a warning here since it's for strong stomachs only but this bare bones trail of blood and guts, about an insane person in clown gear gleefully doing some of the most unthinkably sadistic things to people, is as raw and nerve-wracking as a slasher film can get. This is the one some viewers may tap out of but sometimes it's good to see just how crazy and, in a way, devolved a slasher movie can get.

For a complete Terrifer binge, make sure to watch Terrifier 2 and Terrifier 3 , too.

And that's it for our picks of the best slasher movies of all time! Did your favorite make the cut? Let us know in the comments.

Make sure to check out our picks of the best horror movies and best modern horror movies for even more scary goodness.

Matt Fowler is a freelance entertainment writer/critic, covering TV news, reviews, interviews and features on IGN for 13+ years.

articles.title: The Original Mass Effect Is the Trilogy’s Best Story, Hands Down
articles.summary: The entire Mass Effect trilogy is fantastic, but the first game's story is head-and-shoulders above the tales told in the later games.
articles.body:
UPDATE: This piece was originally written two months ago, but in light of the cancellation of Mass Effect 5 and shuttering of BioWare and the awesome fan movement in progress right now to try and #SaveMassEffect, we're re-sharing this story.

This is an IGN opinion piece from Ryan McCaffrey, who worked at Official Xbox Magazine from 2002-2012 during the original Xbox and Xbox 360 era before joining IGN, where he remains “the Xbox guy.” In the run-up to Xbox’s 25th anniversary, he’ll be sharing his memories from the platform’s first quarter-century.

Anyone old enough to remember the Xbox 360’s earliest days, the ones before Mass Effect finally came out in November of 2007, will recall that BioWare’s epic space opera didn’t just come out of nowhere. It had been hugely anticipated and hyped up a whole lot… and I’m part of the reason why.

I worked at Official Xbox Magazine at the time, and to say we were excited for this RPG would be an understatement. This was a big, big deal. BioWare was, at the time, on a generational run, and Microsoft had signed them to an exclusive deal. Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Jade Empire had already launched as Xbox exclusives, and the studio would go on to create the first two Mass Effect games as 360 exclusives before EA bought it and made it a multiplatform developer. In baseball terms, this was like the Arizona Diamondbacks, as a fledgling expansion team, signing Randy Johnson in 1999 and then watching him go out and promptly win four straight Cy Young Awards and a World Series.

As we approached the mid-point of that four-game exclusive run, BioWare had begun to promise the moon with Mass Effect. It teased a trilogy in which your story choices and progress would carry over from one game to the next and ultimately influence the outcome of the entire story. Not only that, Mass Effect was going to include a serious tech upgrade over BioWare’s previous games, utilizing the stunning Unreal Engine 3 to power its world and characters.

I didn’t get to review Mass Effect at OXM – Fall 2007 for the Xbox 360 was arguably the greatest three-month stretch in gaming history , which meant everyone at OXM was incredibly busy (I’d been assigned to review Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare). The honor went to my colleague, Paul Curthoys, who gave it a well-deserved 10 out of 10 – in-line with IGN’s own 9.4 .

But while I didn’t pen the review, I sure as heck played it. And although I know most people hail Mass Effect 2 as the best in the series, I have always been and will always be a defender of the first game. While yes, its combat was clunkier than the more polished third-person shooting that the sequels brought, for me, the original game’s story is head-and-shoulders above anything in the subsequent games. Shepard’s journey to becoming a Spectre. Meeting classic companions like Wrex and Garrus for the first time and building your relationship with them through your choices (I 100% chose Ashley over Kaidan, how about you?). Exploring the vastness of the Citadel, which was supposed to be this massive hub of the galaxy where alien races from across the galaxy congregated – Mass Effect 1 succeeded in convincing me of that, whereas in Mass Effect 2, the Citadel was reduced to a tiny two-level corridor.

Remember the Elcor? Remember all of the sidequests you could take on? The Citadel was wondrous, and it wasn’t even the most memorable thing about my Mass Effect adventure. That would be the plot twist. Yup, BioWare got me again! I loved where the story went, and Saren was a great villain.

Sure, the framerate struggled to hit 30fps on the Xbox 360, and the elevator rides took forever, but the gameplay and story and world and characters were so damn good in Mass Effect that its technical limitations just didn’t matter. It really was the space opera BioWare had promised. It very clearly could not have been achieved on the previous-generation Xbox. It was genuinely amazing, and it took us on a four-plus-year-ride (Mass Effect 3 shipped in March of 2012 and concluded Shepard’s story) unlike anything we’d ever experienced in gaming before.

Those of you who were there at the time probably remember how awesome your first moments with Mass Effect were, and I hope a new generation gets a chance to experience some version of that with the untitled Mass Effect 5 – even if I’m skeptical that EA’s new venture-capital owners will let BioWare see a single-player game with minimal post-release monetization through to the finish line, especially after it’s already been in development for so long. I hope I’m wrong.

But even if the new Mass Effect never makes it, I’m grateful for the original. It is easily one of the best and most significant Xbox exclusives ever. Whatever Microsoft paid for BioWare’s exclusivity back then, it was worth every cent.

Check out the other notable Xbox games I've looked back on in celebration of the brand's 25th anniversary:

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: Kiah Stokes (again) and officiating among WNBA Finals Game 5 winners and losers
articles.summary: The Valkyries took a 3-2 lead in the WNBA Finals by holding the Dream to a season-low 55 points. Here are the Game 5 winners and losers.
articles.body:
SAN FRANCISCO — The Golden State Valkyries have the upper hand in the WNBA Finals.

The franchise, which is in its second season of existence, is one game away from it's first title after a 64-55 victory over the Atlanta Dream on Monday, Oct. 26, at the Chase Center. They now hold a 3-2 lead in the best-of-seven series.

It was a defensive battle as the Valkyries held the Dream to a season-low 55 points. Atlanta shot 29% from the field gave up 21 points on 17 turnovers.

Kiah Stokes continued her MVP-worthy performance with 13 points, eight rebounds and three blocks. Veronica Burton had near identical line with 13 points, eight rebounds and four blocks. Cecilia Zandalasini and Tiffany Hayes added 12 points each.

"I want to win and to win, I wanna beat the best and these are some of the best players in the league, especially this series," Stokes said "And I don't know, I just take the challenge.

"I think our whole team, they rely on me, they give me energy, they give me confidence. And yeah, I'm just trying to do what I can to help the team in any way possible."

Here are the winners and losers from Game 5 of the WNBA Finals:

WNBA Finals Game 5 photos as Valkyries and Dream fight on

The Golden State Valkyries blocked nine shots in Game 5 and in the process set a new WNBA Finals record with 37 blocks in a single series.

Valkyries point guard Veronica Burton set a postseason career high with four blocks and tied Diana Taurasi for the most blocks by a guard in a WNBA Finals game. Center Kiah Stokes had her sixth straight games with at least three blocks, tied with Lisa Leslie for the longest streak in a single postseason in WNBA playoff history.

Both teams packed the paint on defense. Although Stokes served as the primary anchor down low for Golden State, Burton did a phenomenal job rotating and assuming position as the last line of defense under the basket. The Valkyries limited the Dream to 9-of-33 shooting in the paint, including 3-of-12 in the second half.

Valkyries center Kiah Stokes has been borderline unstoppable on the defensive side of the ball. That didn't change on Monday, where she recorded three blocks in Golden State's Game 5 win — her fifth consecutive game with three or more blocks in the WNBA Finals.

Stokes also flexed her offensive capabilities. Although the 6-foot-3 center said she was "just shooting it," Stokes connected on 3-of-4 attempts from beyond the arc. Stokes finished with 13 points, her highest scoring performance in the entire postseason.

"To be honest, (Tiffany Hayes) cussed me out when I passed up one (shot), so I didn't want to make her mad again," joked Stokes, who rounded out her stat line with eight rebounds and one assist.

Veronica Burton said the Valkyries would not be in the position they are in without Stokes.

"Seriously, what she does on a daily basis and she asks for nothing in return. She's one of the most humble people I've ever met," Burton said. "It's more than just defense. I know everyone wants to talk about defense with Kiah, but it's offense too and she contributes on both sides of the ball. So we're really happy to have her."

Celebrities show up in style for an unforgettable WNBA Finals

Valkyries guard Veronica Burton's aggressiveness

Veronica Burton wasn't just struggling throughout the series. It seemed like her confidence was in limbo, second-guessing when to drive, pass or shoot. She looked deep within herself for a spark, had the reassurance of teammates and turned in her best game of the series.

Big Shot Burton, as the Bay Area fans affectionately call her, finished with 13 points (on 5-of-15 shooting), eight rebounds and four blocks, a WNBA Finals record (tied with Diana Taurasi) for most blocks in a game by a guard.

"It's the team and the confidence that they pour into me. I really feel it," Burton said. "It's so hard to perform if you don't feel like people have your back, around you. And it's so easy to perform when you feel like they have your back. And that's what it is here. Like, it is so much love and just so much, like, energy poured into you that you just feel invincible almost."

Through five games in the WNBA Finals, Burton is averaging 9.0 points, 4.8 rebounds, 3.4 assists and 1.8 blocks per game.

The Valkyries have played great defense but the referees have missed enough calls, according to Atlanta Dream coach Karl Smesko, that he took them to task in defense of Angel Reese after Game 5 — which is notable, considering his even-keel nature.

"I give them credit for playing good defense," Smesko said. "But I mean, I do want to have Angel's back here. The contact they allow on Angel compared to everybody else is just ridiculous. It's just ridiculous. And we should have gone to the foul line six to eight more times just on that.

"To miss double dribbles and travels, multiple that always led to points, man, you can't be at this level and make that many mistakes. ... And it's time that if you push somebody with two hands as they drive, it's got to be a foul. And I'm kind of tired of some of the excuses that I'm hearing."

Reese made Finals history with three straight double-doubles through the first three games of the series and has been limited to less than 10 points in the Dream's back-to-back losses.

She said Monday night officials have even missed intentional fouls on her, and noted the shift in the calls started after the Dream established a 2-1 lead.

Golden State coach Natalie Nakase, when asked about the physicality, noted contact is bound to happen between two defensive-minded teams.

In the fourth quarter alone, Atlanta had more turnovers (7) than field goals (5). The Dream barely ended the game in the black with 19 made field goals and 17 turnovers (tied with Finals Game 4 for the team's most this postseason) were extremely costly.

Atlanta attempted 65 shots to Golden State's 61 but conceded 21 points off turnovers – accounting for almost a third of Golden State's total points. In a series where shooting is at a premium, those giveaways add up fast.

The Dream bench registered four points, all scored by Isobel Borlase. DeWanna Bonner was held scoreless in 13 minutes, shooting 0-of-2 from the 3-point line. Dream head coach Karl Smesko gave Te-Hinea Paopao and Madina Okot some minutes in the first half in search of some production, before trimming the rotation back to seven players.

As the Dream starters continue to log heavy minutes across this best-of-seven series — Rhyne Howard played 38 minutes in Game 5 — Atlanta will need someone on their bench to step up.

In comparison, Golden State has the highest-scoring bench of the regular season. Natalie Nakase didn't play Janelle Salaun, the 2026 Sixth Woman of the Year, in Game 5, but the Valkyries showed their strength in numbers with 15 bench points. Cecilia Zandalasini led all reserves with 12 points off the bench.

articles.title: Kevin Cash Reacts to Rays Blowout Loss to Brewers in Game 3
articles.summary: Tampa Bay Rays manager Kevin Cash shared his reaction after his team’s blowout loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of the World Series.Tampa Bay lost 10-...
articles.body:
Tampa Bay Rays manager Kevin Cash shared his reaction after his team's blowout loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of the World Series.

Tampa Bay lost 10-1 on Monday night at home in Game 3 of the World Series, and the team is now down big in the World Series as the Brewers have a 3-0 lead.

With that in mind, the Rays must now win the remaining four games of the series if they are going to accomplish their ultimate goal of winning the franchise's World Series, one that seems to be slipping away.

Speaking to reporters following the Rays' 10-1 loss in Game 3 of the World Series, Cash shared his reaction to the lopsided defeat by dropping a very direct quote.

"It's definitely deflating. How could it not be?" Cash said.

When asked what the Rays need to do to turn the series around, Cash could only say that the team needs to take things one game at a time and grab a win in Game 4 on Tuesday night to force a Game 5.

"The only thing we can do is win tomorrow," Cash said.

Now that the Brewers have a 3-0 series lead, the sportsbooks do not like Tampa Bay's chances of coming back and winning the World Series.

According to DraftKings Sportsbook , Milwaukee is a -5000 favorite to win the World Series, with the Rays +1500 underdogs to come back and win it.

Those odds imply that Milwaukee has about a 98% chance of winning the World Series, meaning that Tampa Bay is truly on the ropes right now as they look to keep their championship odds alive.

Although the Rays were the best team in the American League this year, the Brewers appear to be just a cut above them, and every other team in the league, for that matter, as they continue to buzzsaw their way through the playoffs.

That being said, the series is not over yet, and we play seven games for a reason. So, although the task is tall, the Rays still have a chip and a chair.

articles.title: Brewers’ Pat Murphy keeps Milwaukee on its toes with statement amid 3-0 lead vs. Rays
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers are one win away from the first World Series title in franchise history, but Pat Murphy is not about to let his team get comfortable a...
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers are one win away from the first World Series title in franchise history , but Pat Murphy is not about to let his team get comfortable against the Tampa Bay Rays.

After Milwaukee's 10-1 rout in Game 3 on Monday night at Tropicana Field gave the Brewers a commanding 3-0 series lead, Murphy praised his club's relentlessness while making it clear the job is not done.

"I mean, the guys play hard. You know, it's evident the guys play hard. They just, you know, they don't give in. And they make every pitch count, and that's what it takes to win," Murphy said, via FOX Sports . "And that's the same thing that Tampa did all year, you know. That team is very, very capable."

Murphy acknowledged his team is in a great spot, but he was not ready to call the series.

"This is a best-of-seven series. So, it looks like we're in the driver's seat, but that doesn't, you know, it's baseball. Anything can happen," Murphy said. "But I like the way we battle."

His team certainly battled on Monday. After taking a 2-0 lead in the third, Milwaukee broke the game open with an eight-run fifth inning , with every run scoring with two outs. Brice Turang's two-run single was part of a string of seven straight two-out hits, making it one of the biggest innings in World Series history.

Jackson Chourio led the way with four hits , while Christian Yelich kept the inning alive by beating out a force play that was overturned on replay. Milwaukee finished with 16 hits.

Robert Gasser was just as dominant on the mound. The left-hander tossed six shutout innings and allowed just one hit while facing the minimum. He joined Don Larsen, who threw a perfect game in 1956, as the only pitchers in World Series history to go six-plus innings while facing the minimum. Rays starter Freddy Peralta, meanwhile, failed to get through five innings.

The Brewers, now 10-1 this postseason, can clinch the title with a win in Game 4 on Tuesday night.

Murphy added that his club has shown it can pounce on any opening.

"You give them an inch, sometimes they break through and keep going," Murphy said.

articles.title: Pokemon Unite to Be Taken Offline in 2027, In-Game Sales Suspended Immediately
articles.summary: Pokemon Unite will end service on March 23, 2027, following the game’s final competition, the Aeos Crown 2027, just two days prior in Tokyo.
articles.body:
Pokemon Unite will end service on March 23, 2027, following the game’s final competition, the Aeos Crown 2027, just two days prior in Tokyo. The MOBA Pokemon battler will be shut down on both Nintendo Switch and mobile.

According to The Pokemon Company, Aeos Gem sales have been halted immediately along with any new Unite Club memberships and automatic renewals.

“We offer our sincerest gratitude to the many Trainers who have played since service started for the Nintendo Switch version on July 21, 2021,” said the announcement. “We hope you continue to enjoy Pokémon Unite until the final day of service.”

Once the game closes, players will be able to view their stats and achievements, and even play practice rounds, but online matches won’t be available. To do so, you’ll need to download a new library feature.

"Even after service ends, players who complete the required library data download before Tuesday, March 23, 2027, at 00:00 UTC will be able to use the library feature to view certain records and in-game content,” the announcement said. “Players who do not complete the required download before service ends will not be able to use the library feature afterward.”

Many expected the news after Pokemon Unite was conspicuously absent from the Pokemon World Championships 2027 ’s list of games. The final update lands in November, along with a special event where players can grab Unite licenses, Holowear, and other items.

Pokémon Unite was originally released on July 21, 2021, for the Nintendo Switch, and on September 22, 2021, for Android and iOS mobile devices.

IGN’s 6/10 Pokemon Unite review called it “an entertaining casual MOBA constrained by its overcommitment to simplicity (and some questionable microtransactions).” At least those are gone now.

Here’s a list of every Pokemon game you can play on Switch right now . We’ll update that when Unite ends service in 2027.

articles.title: Acer is bringing a Predator gaming handheld to the US for the first time
articles.summary: The Predator Atlas 8 is coming to Best Buy on November 1st, and will cost $1,300 at launch.
articles.body: It’s been several months since Acer unveiled its Predator Atlas 8 gaming handheld, but now we finally know that it’s coming to the US, and how much it’ll cost. The Intel Arc G3 Extreme variant — the more powerful of the two models announced in May — will be available exclusively at Best Buy on November 1st, priced at $1,299.99. For that, the Atlas 8 provides Arc B390 graphics with 12 Xe3 GPU cores, paired with 24GB of LPDDR5x RAM. The 8-inch display runs at 120Hz, and the device comes equipped with dual-mode triggers, TMR joysticks, and the ability to be used for both handheld or docked setups. It runs Windows 11 and can be used with Xbox Game Pass, so there’s no shortage of supported games you can play. While Acer has announced a bunch of handheld gaming devices under its Predator and Nitro series, this is the first to receive an official US launch. It’s the same price as the Xbox Ally X20 and is seemingly already proving popular, given the preorders that Best Buy launched last week are already sold out. Acer said online orders will open again on November 1st alongside in-store availability.

articles.title: Silent Hill Remake Coming 2027, First Cast Details Leaked
articles.summary: The 1999 PS1 horror game is getting the Bloober treatment, and a new leak from MP1ST suggests work has been underway since 2022 and the game is targeting a 2027 launch.
articles.body:
With Silent Hill 2’s remake selling 6 million copies , it’s no surprise Bloober Team and Konami would want to have another crack at things. Last year, the Polish developer and Japanese publisher confirmed they were doing just that with a remake of the first Silent Hill .

The 1999 PS1 horror game is getting the Bloober treatment, and a new leak from MP1ST suggests work has been underway since 2022 and the game is targeting a 2027 launch.

According to the report, the game cast its actors under the codename “Project Noise,” and features Gabrielle Fritz and Jade Matthew in major roles.

Fritz has worked in other games, from Battlefield 2042 to Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossus, as well as a range of TV shows. Matthew is best known for British TV appearances.

While it isn’t clear what roles the two actors play in Silent Hill’s remake, the report speculated that police officer Cybil Bennett, nurse Lisa Garland, or primary antagonist Dahlia Gillespie would fit. There’s no word on who could play protagonist Harry Mason yet.

Bloober Team is also working on DLC for Cronos: The New Dawn, its multiplayer horror game, Saw: Genesis, and story-driven adventure Star Trek: Shadow Frontier.

The 2027 release window lines up with Konami’s recent spate of Silent Hill projects, with Townfall launching this year and Silent Hill f in 2025, giving us a new Silent Hill project each year. You can check out the games in order in our Silent Hill timeline .

Konami is planning "second and third waves" of new Silent Hill games , according to producer Motoi Okamoto, who pointed at Silent Hill 2 Remake, Silent Hill f, and Silent Hill: Townfall as the first wave.

That would make a remake of the first game the beginning of the second wave of new Silent Hill projects. It’ll be interesting to see what comes after.

articles.title: Mass Effect Has Been Taken Away Just When We Needed It Most
articles.summary: Mass Effect: Universe looked great, and BioWare's closure means it's been taken away just when we needed it most.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Carlos Morales. Mass Effect is his favorite game series, and he even wrote his major research paper for his Master’s degree on it.

For the past week, all of Council space has been in an uproar over the shuttering of beloved RPG studio BioWare and the subsequent cancelling of Mass Effect 5. The next game in the acclaimed science-fiction saga, tentatively titled Mass Effect: Universe as revealed by a leaked trailer , will now seemingly never be finished. To say that the corporate overlords at Electronic Arts have done a disservice to their employees and gamers all over would be a tremendous understatement. Both those in the game’s development and fans of the franchise have made their displeasure known to the tune of numerous opinion pieces and over 200,000 signatures for a petition to save the series from limbo. Avi Lewis, the leader of Canada’s New Democratic Party, has even weighed in on the matter by saying the Canadian government should intervene and save the studio.

Whether these efforts will bear fruit is anyone’s guess, but the backlash is some of the worst I’ve seen for a gaming-related controversy in a while, perhaps aside from the PlayStation disc debacle. Mass Effect may not have been the most lucrative franchise to ever hit store shelves, but its popularity is plain to see from the passionate outcry. People love Mass Effect, they love BioWare, and they want to see what the studio was cooking with their latest entry. Instead, the studio was sacrificed at the altar of private equity debt, robbing the many to benefit the few. But to make matters even more tragic, the details we have learned about Mass Effect: Universe make it seem like it would’ve been the perfect game for where we are culturally in 2026.

Mass Effect: Next Chapter Game Award Trailer Screenshots

When Mass Effect 3 launched in 2012, fan reception was incredibly polarized due to the much maligned ending to Commander Shepard’s journey. Despite unanimously positive critical reviews, it took the Extended Cut DLC and a long cooling-down period for a lot of fans to come around to the game’s strengths. I don’t like the ending either, but the vast majority of Mass Effect 3 is a fantastic experience, and in many ways it was ahead of its time in terms of how it anticipated the cultural anxieties of the 2020s.

For those not in the know, Mass Effect 3 features a world at war with the Reapers, a seemingly unstoppable race of techno-organic starships. The Reapers have arrived to exterminate all intelligent life in the galaxy, and basically the entire game is a gauntlet in the face of utter annihilation, with little in the way of hope or relief. Player character Commander Shepard may be a symbol for the galactic community’s resistance, but the overall tone of Mass Effect 3 is unlike any game I’ve ever played.

A profound melancholy and defeatism are baked into the game’s writing. It seems almost everyone understands deep down that this is the end of the world, or at least of the one we know. The Reapers destroy galactic civilization every 50,000 years, and they have never failed once in countless cycles. The chance of humanity’s survival is small, and even if Shepard succeeds, what the galaxy would look like after such a devastating war is hard to conceive. Friends and allies try to support each other, but the looming despair is impossible to ignore. Even Shepard’s potential victories, like curing the genophage virus afflicting the Krogan or brokering a peace treaty between the Geth and Quarians, feel like drops in the ocean compared to the dozens of worlds and billions of casualties crushed beneath the Reapers’ tentacled heels — brief moments of peace before the loudest bang of all.

Mass Effect 3’s overwhelming sense of fatalism, of trying to hold on to hope in a world without a future, feels more resonant now than it did in 2012. The 2020s have been a turbulent decade, with numerous potentially world-ending catastrophes either ongoing or just beyond the horizon. Between climate change, COVID-19, perpetual violence in the Middle East, the rise of generative AI, and unchecked late-stage capitalism, the last several years have been a nonstop cavalcade of disasters. The damage to the social contract and the realization that we’re probably all traumatized and a little bit insane is difficult to process, especially when the soaring cost of living forces people to still go to work and act like everything is normal while the world crumbles around them.

But now that we have more details about Mass Effect: Universe, it sounds like it would have been an artistic antidote to the contemporary mindset. Set 600 years after the Reaper War, the game would have depicted a galaxy that’s picked up the pieces after such widespread destruction. New alliances and factions have risen, and even the Batarians, a race that was said to be almost extinct during Mass Effect 3, have survived to the new era. Liara T’Soni, one of the most prominent of Shepard’s companions, was set to return as an asari matriarch who’s now witnessed nearly a millennium of strife but is still fighting the good fight.

Mass Effect: Andromeda’s solution to continuing the Mass Effect story after the cataclysmic events of Mass Effect 3 was to sidestep them; to have a new cast jump ship to another galaxy before the end of everything. By contrast, Mass Effect: Universe was going to tackle the problem head-on, with the developers challenging themselves to imagine what rebuilding after the apocalypse really looks like. We’ve only seen small glimpses of their solution, but a game that shows there was a path forward after the Reapers would likely resonate with people while we’re still in the trenches of the mid-2020s. Whether players picked up on it subconsciously or otherwise, Mass Effect: Universe had the potential to give people hope that we can persevere through the psycho reality we’re currently living in.

Mass Effect: Universe would not have solved the problems facing today’s world, but art does provide an outlet to reflect on and process one’s day-to-day experience. “Your words are as empty as your future,” says Reaper villain Sovereign in the first Mass Effect. It sure would’ve been nice to play something that offers a counterargument.

Carlos Morales writes novels, articles, and Mass Effect essays. You can follow his fixations on Twitter .

articles.title: Kingdom Come: Deliverance Developer Hit by 'Serious' Cybersecurity Incident
articles.summary: Warhorse Studios — the developer behind Kingdom Come: Deliverance, its sequel and an upcoming Lord of the Rings RPG — has been hit by a “serious” cyberattack.
articles.body:
Warhorse Studios — the developer behind Kingdom Come: Deliverance, its sequel, and an upcoming Lord of the Rings RPG — has been hit by a “serious” cyberattack. The company announced the news on its website .

The developer is currently working with cybersecurity experts to “secure its systems, investigate the incident, and assess its full impact.” Warhorse has also reached out to authorities to track down the culprits, who accessed company systems and data.

“This is a serious incident for Warhorse Studios and everyone affected,” said Martin Frývaldský, CEO of Warhorse Studios. “Our immediate priority is to secure our systems, establish the full extent of the breach, and take the necessary steps to protect our employees, partners, and community.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 Legacy of the Forge DLC Screenshots

“We are dedicating the resources needed to address this situation and will communicate further information as soon as we responsibly can.”

Warhorse said it won’t comment further or conduct any interviews on the topic, so the extent of the attack isn’t clear at the moment. The studio will share updates as it can.

Warhorse Studios is currently working on a Lord of the Rings role-playing game, described as an “open world Middle-earth RPG,” and a new Kingdom Come game expected to be Kingdom Come: Deliverance 3 or a spinoff.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 launched last year to critical and commercial acclaim. IGN's Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 review returned a 9/10. We said: "Armed with excellent melee combat and an exceptional story, Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is one part sequel and one part coronation, bringing a lot of the original's ideas to fruition."

While Warhorse has enjoyed significant success with Kingdom Come: Deliverance, it has come under fire recently for its use of generatve AI . Daniel Vávra, the previous director of Kingdom Come: Deliverance, stepped down from his role in February to focus on making a Kingdom Come: Deliverance movie .

This month, Japanese developer Capcom was also hit with a cyberattack which saw 196 customer accounts compromised. Retailer Playasia was also taken offline . These hacks coincide with what security experts have dubbed “Black October” in which AI agents have disrupted internet security. It isn’t clear if Capcom, Playasai, or the Warhorse hack is related to that.

articles.title: Riftbound’s New Radiance Booster Set Brings an Awesome New Music Component to the League of Legends TCG
articles.summary: Get an early look at League of Legends Riftbound's upcoming Radiance expansion.
articles.body:
Riftbound, the League of Legends card game, caps off the year with its latest booster set, Radiance. This marks the fifth set in the TCG, and a highly anticipated collaboration with Riot Games Music. In addition to some fan favorite iterations of Legends, we’re of course introduced to some new mechanics and new Legends, like Evelynn and the IGN-exclusively-revealed Mordekaiser. We’re also getting another two-player constructed starter kit in the form of the Evelynn and Seraphine showdown decks. As a fan of Riot Games Music and groups like K/DA , this set is looking to be an exciting drop not just for players but for a whole different segment within the Riot fanbase.

Arguably, the most exciting addition of every new set are the new mechanics to play around with. In Radiance, we have three new keywords with Deploy, Show Off, and Disarm. Deploy is another take on gear that focuses heavily on battlefield control versus activating abilities at base or equipping attachments directly onto units. For example, the Bushwhack Trap gear allows the owner or ally controlling the associated battlefield to play another hidden card there, even though the limit is usually one per battlefield. Show Off allows players to reveal a card from their hand or choose a friendly card on the field to activate its abilities to a certain degree. The spell Rousing Display may have the player reveal a card of energy cost 7 or more to gain the full effect. If the criteria is successfully met, Rousing Display plays four token units instead of two. And Disarm is probably the most straightforward addition, being the opposite of Assault where units with Disarm lower an enemy’s might on attack rather than empowering their own might. I especially like the new Deploy keyword in gear, as it makes for some inconvenient scenarios for your opponent if you can hold the battlefield. It’s another layer of risk and reward to think about when taking into account the timing of movement. It’s also a nice touch to balance this new type of gear by having the simple act of holding a battlefield to get rid of an opponent’s deployed gear, considering gear removal isn’t as readily available as removal for units. Overall, there’s a nice mix of keywords this time around that I’m enjoying so far.

As always, the two-player kit of showdown decks is a good way for new players to jump right into the game and showcase the hot new mechanics and Legends. For Radiance, we have the new Evelynn (Body and Chaos) vs Seraphine (Mind and Order) Showdown Decks. After getting a few matches piloting both, the Evelynn deck is probably my favorite of the two, focusing on hiding cards for extra benefits. For example, the Evelynn Agony’s Embrace Legend allows the player to draw a card if a hidden or facedown card is revealed for the first time that turn. This alongside the battlefield, Bandle Scouts’ Academy, which has a player gain a Gold gear token when hiding a card there adds an extra resource edge. Furthermore, the champion unit Evelynn In Control can score an additional point if she holds a battlefield with a facedown card. With the possibility of holding battlefields quickly while gaining extra resources to play hidden cards, this Evelynn deck can really get ahead without falling behind on runes too much. The Seraphine deck is still a contender, though, focusing more on going wide and playing a ton of units for optimizing the effects of their cards. For example, the Seraphine Starry-Eyed Songstress Legend has an ability to exhaust herself and three friendly units to reduce the cost of a spell by two mana or runes. Another cool card in the deck is the champion unit Seraphine Not Alone, who plays a 1 might recruit when she’s played or exhausted via moving or another different ability. In addition she gains +1 might for every other exhausted unit the player controls. So this Seraphine unit can get really buff as long as the exhausted units stay alive on the field. Similarly, the spell card High Note benefits from exhausted units the player controls. When played, the player can give a unit negative might for every exhausted unit they control. It’s great synergy if you can keep these lowly tokens around long enough. For me, the Seraphine deck was just a bit slower to set up than the Evelynn deck. Not to mention the Show Off keyword emphasis in the deck meant having more high energy cost cards in my hand that I wasn’t able to use often enough on curve since I was focusing on going wide. Either way I see the potential in both decks to be tweaked enough for a competitive scene.

Now the biggest question for many players getting into the new competitive season: which new cards should I use in my decks? First off, there are some high-performing meta decks from the last set to consider taking into the Radiance meta. Irelia Blade Dancer is one in particular that’s still a fan favorite with Calm(green) and Chaos(purple). This is a spell heavy deck that focuses on unit survivability while being nimble to gain benefits. To keep with the spells and movement trend, the Satchel Charge card is a good choice to add. In addition to moving a friendly unit, the player can play a bomb token on a battlefield. The bomb token serves as another threat if the opposing player tries to hold. Another good spell card is Hush, which counters expensive cost cards. Sometimes the opposing player just needs a big out, and Hush is a good way to kill that momentum shift. In regards to survivability, the Resplendent Rostrum gear could be a good add, giving not only a +3 might buff to a unit, but also a refresh to your hand and rune count.

Another current meta deck that could carry over into Radiance is Azir Emperor of the Sands in Calm(green) and Order(yellow). This deck focuses on equipment and Azir’s Sand Soldier tokens. It’s pretty wild to run next to no units in this deck, but it works. Azir’s ability is so unique that it’s tough to stray away from the current deck brews out there. So in terms of Radiance cards, spells would fit best since we don’t have much equipment to work with in these two colors. There are some new spells that synergize with gear, making perfect additions to this deck. The first being Battle Preparations, which gives +2 might to a unit. But if you Show Off a gear card, which is fairly easy in this deck, the player can ready up two runes, thus making this spell free in the end. The other ideal spell to consider is Command: Attack, which allows the player to look at the top 5 cards of the deck and reveal a gear to add to their hand. There’s a secondary ability for gear with the Deploy keyword, but that isn’t the best use in this Azir deck. And Raucous Anthem is another spell with potential that readies the player’s units and gives them +3 might for the turn. It may help with a game-changing big push, including any new Sand Soldier token units that were just played that turn. There are not too many new cards to consider, but the small tweaks can be a net positive.

Even though the Mordekaiser seems like a promising Legend in this set, the one that intrigues me the most is Ziggs Hexplosives Expert, who has the ability to play a bomb token to any battlefield. The idea of littering bomb tokens across both battlefields sounds like a good time. Not only do they possibly prevent the opposing players from holding consistently, they’ll most likely lose some units just to get rid of the bombs. So while you’re laying these traps, you can set up or even get ahead on conquers and holds if they don’t want to risk losing their units to contest. Explosimian is a great example of explosive pressure adding three bomb tokens to a battlefield whenever they hold. Alongside Ziggs Short-Fused, each bomb token does an extra damage. So potentially, Explosimian can set up nine damage if the opposing player decides to take the risk of occupying a battlefield. It doesn’t stop scoring via holds, but players will have to rebuild their board state if they don’t have an answer to these bombs. Speaking of answers, units with Deflect is the obvious counter here by making players pay an additional mana to target with bombs, but I’d still try the Legend out anyway. Maybe the competition will least expect it. The Fury(red) and Chaos(purple) of Ziggs also reminds me of Draven, so there might be some cards there that transfer over fairly easily like Falling Star to finish off what the bombs couldn’t or Kai-Sa Survivor with the potential open battlefields after bomb activations.

As a band geek and fan of Riot Games Music, the music-themed special and overnumbered cards of Radiance speak to me. When Riftbound first released, I had a chance to talk to Dave Guskin, the Game Director, and one of the many questions I asked was when K/DA would show up. Of course, he was very aware of their popularity among others and it was very much a possibility. Now they’re here in the Radiance set alongside the group HEARTSTEEL and some sleek-looking runes featuring instruments to boot. In another IGN interview with Riftbound executive producer Chengran Chai, he mentioned that they “...knew Riot as a whole would have a music moment towards the end of the year, so very early on, we said we would lean into that.” Now with K/DA dropping their new song FIRESTARTER alongside some new looks, Riftbound has also celebrated the new release with a Couture Collection collaboration. Overall, this “music moment” in Riftbound is one of my favorites of the game so far.

From the new mechanics and Legends to the Riot Games Music representation with K/DA and HEARTSTEEL, Radiance is an exciting set for players, collectors, and even fans of the music groups. The new keywords have potential to make a major change in how players interact with battlefields, and the music collaborations brings in a new type of fan into the Riftbound community. There’s a lot to chew on this set from a competitive and collector point of view, and I look forward to seeing how it shakes out going into the new year. For more on Riftbound, check out our hands-on impressions of the last set Vendetta , and also our interview with Riftbound executive producer Chengran Chai about the Radiance set.

Mike Mamon is a Syndication & Digital Specialist at IGN, devil fruit user, and world-renown JoJo poser. Let's chat anime or TCGs on Bluesky @xpmnms.bsky.social

articles.title: The Wolf Among Us Remastered Review - IGN
articles.summary: A brilliant way to either revisit or catch up on a neo-noir mystery that still deserves its flowers.
articles.body:
With intense performances, a heady atmosphere, and sharp writing, The Wolf Among Us’ gripping neo-noir saga rivalled the prestige TV dramas of the time when it first came out in 2013, earning acclaim as one of Telltale’s greatest yet. Now, with a long-awaited sequel in the works, it’s been given a fresh coat of paint that’s gussied up locations and added a slew of behind-the-scenes content to sweeten the pot. Some holdover annoyances haven’t been addressed, like the original’s stiff and occasionally uncanny animations, which get in the way of The Wolf Among Us Remastered feeling truly definitive. Still, this story remains a fantastic one, and the enhanced set dressing even manages to deepen its sinister mood.

For those who didn’t play the original, The Wolf Among Us thoughtfully adapts Bill Willingham’s beloved graphic novel series Fables, in which folklore characters covertly coexist with humans in a New York suburb aptly called Fabletown. Set roughly 20 years earlier as a non-canon prequel, Telltale’s adaptation artfully draws on classic noir storytelling, dropping you into the shoes of Sheriff Bigby (aka the Big Bad Wolf) to solve a bizarre but gripping murder. With a decapitated head on his stoop and little more to go on than a ribbon and an etched ring, the marshal must use his keen nose and perception to find the culprit… and he has to do it fast. With humans investigating the case and the social fabric of the mythical community at stake, failure could cause their secret society to collapse entirely.

The Wolf Among Us Remastered Screenshots

On top of that already immense pressure, there’s one more important piece of subtext to consider: after centuries of violence as a storybook baddie, Bigby’s constituents don’t necessarily trust him to get the job done and, naturally, watch his every move. As such, he’s forced to lean on familiar faces like Snow White, The Little Mermaid, and Bufkin from The Wizard of Oz to chase leads as he unravels a web of complex issues spanning class consciousness, poverty, and abuses of power. It’s a journey that proves to be thoroughly engrossing.

To peel back the seedy underbelly of Fabletown, your time as Bigby is loosely split into segments. For the most part, you’ll have intriguing conversations from a third-person perspective, choosing from a handful of responses as a clock quickly ticks down. Through this system, you can lean on witnesses who seem to be hiding something, threatening them if they continue to hold back. Or, if all else fails, you can resort to physical violence (assuming that aligns with your own moral compass). Cleverly, the language used in these interactions draws on its fairy tale source material without ever feeling corny. So, despite including terms like Witching Well and Magic Mirror, the conversations remain emotionally charged – a tribute to the writing underneath and the resonant, enduring performances of its cast.

What’s most important is that your reactions here are not one-sided. As you make certain decisions, a threatening notification pops up stating that the character you’re interacting with will remember what you did (a staple of the genre). For example, say you make a promise to deliver something and don’t come through – well, they might have a few choice words for you the next time you meet. In this way, The Wolf Among Us is not just about solving the whodunit; it is also about choosing whether Bigby will shake off his villainous origins and prove his status as Sheriff and protector.

What’s neat is that the choice is mostly up to you. If you want to, you can cruelly push the citizens to get your answers, or try as often as you might to take their side, even if that means going against the legal institution to which you are professionally bound. By exploring this curious grey area, I began to understand why the residents of Fabletown act as they do, eventually allowing me to empathise with their actions, no matter how desperate or depraved they may be.

Amidst these social calls, you’ll occasionally control Bigby directly as he picks through dingy locations – such as dive bars and ornate offices – interacting with clues to advance the investigation. Just like in conversations, there are even more ethical quandaries to consider, like whether you should interrupt a wake like an unemotional jerk or kick in a door instead of knocking like a gentleman. As the confusing haze of right and wrong settled in, I frequently struggled to maintain my good-guy persona, especially when provoked. It would be so easy to smack an obvious bad guy in the head to get the answers I needed more quickly, but then wouldn’t I be just as bad as him?

Last but not least are the interactive sequences, which require you to complete a series of quick time events to survive some of the higher octane moments throughout the tale. You’ll rip out throats, jump across city blocks, and even set broken bones, with failure occasionally leading to a game over. Thankfully, frequent checkpoints drop you right back into the action if you miss a beat. The variety and frequency of these moments do well to keep you busy as you piece together the killer's identity, particularly as many of them arrive with mesmerising (and sometimes gruesome) animations.

Mirroring the flow of the original, The Wolf Among Us Remastered takes place over five episodes that are about two hours long (all included in this single package instead of being sold individually). For the most part, the choices you make feel impactful, which keeps the momentum chugging along nicely. That is, until the penultimate episode, when the pace suddenly dips and characters start needlessly reiterating their points of view. In earlier episodes, I’d look under every stone to figure out who the villain was, and I was fairly confident I understood what was going on by episode four, so everything slowing down right when I was ready for the payoff felt slightly disjointed.

I do get why they didn’t alter this chapter more substantially; this is a remaster, not a remake, and major story alterations could ultimately do more harm than good if handled poorly. Besides, there are still enjoyable chats throughout the episode, so the dragging is only a minor blip in an otherwise brilliant story, with a finale that certainly clawed me back. But when the rest of the tale is so tight and considered, it’s still a bit annoying to spend a couple of hours rehashing information you’ve already worked hard to uncover.

That dissatisfaction is also softened by the fact that the locations you visit are so intentionally designed and brilliantly reflect the personalities of their inhabitants. While Bigby's tiny, sparsely furnished flat fits with his lone wolf status, the local watering hole’s scrappy yet warm atmosphere matches its down-on-their-luck clientele. The remaster's design glow-up further bolsters that environmental storytelling, as everything from couch upholstery to pawn shop artefacts has been redesigned with far more detail. For instance, those familiar with Aunt Greenleaf's apartment will see that it’s now even witchier than before, with hanging tassels and strewn curios. Elsewhere, the infamous Puddin ‘n’ Pie remains seedy but stylish, featuring Art Nouveau-esque pendant lights and extravagant neon piping.

With so much effort spent on the look, it’s a shame that not every detail received the same touch, and that there are still a handful of friction points on the technical side. Characters sometimes move as if on a swivel, and Bigby’s animations when finding clues tend to feel strangely rigid and occasionally robotic. In the 2013 original, these blips were passable, but in a 2026 remaster, the awkward animations and jerky movements stand out. That’s not to say they are so distracting that they undo all the impressive polishing elsewhere, just that I wish those edges had been similarly smoothed over in order to soundly mark this as the definitive version of the tale.

Harkening back to a simpler era of DVD extras, The Wolf Among Us Remastered also includes a gaggle of bonus features for fans who might want a peek behind the curtain of development. There’s a toggleable Noir game mode that lets you play out the tale in black and white, a digital gallery that compares old art stills with new ones, plus developer and cast interviews about the making-of. As someone who likes to sift through every scrap of lore, I found these additions certainly fun to pilfer through… even if the interface is a tad old-fashioned, leaning more toward sentiment than usefulness. The most compelling add by far is a handful of playable deleted scenes that, while rough around the edges, highlight interesting plot threads and deviations that are exciting to experience after the final credits roll.

articles.title: BioWare Can Never Die: It’s Everywhere You Look - IGN
articles.summary:
BioWare doesn’t need a eulogy: as private equity and corporate consolidation shutters yet another legendary creative institution, the social media has naturally flooded with obituaries for the studio behind Mass Effect, Dragon Age, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic. But you cannot kill BioWare by filing some legal paperwork: it is the foundational DNA of modern interactive storytelling, and massively influential in the wider world of culture, seeping into everything from Star Trek to The Expanse. BioWare has attained a level of mortality that most storytellers can only dream of: by outliving its corporate shell and quietly conquering an entire medium.
BioWare's design philosophy continues to drive the biggest RPGs, and more besides. Its spiritual successors include Archetype Entertainment’s sci-fi epic Exodus (helmed by Drew Karpyshyn and James Ohlen), Casey Hudson’s Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic at Arcanaut Studios, Mike Laidlaw’s Eternal Strands, and David Gaider’s Stray Gods. BioWare’s cinematic dialogue systems, Aurora Engine, and narrative flair set the blueprint for masterpieces like CD Projekt Red’s The Witcher 3 and Larian Studios' Baldur’s Gate 3, while inspiring other genres like sports simulation, racing, and turn-based strategy to adopt BioWare-style story mechanics.
