articles.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Shakes Things Up for Season 3 With a Time Jump and ‘The Orc with an Arc’
articles.summary: IGN visited the set of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power in England back in August 2025 where we got the scoop on what's in store for Middle-earth in the show's upcoming third season.
articles.body:
“There's a lot going on right now,” The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power co-showrunner Patrick McKay told me on the set in England in August 2025.

At the moment, McKay is catching his breath as the crew resets to shoot a quiet but key moment from the Prime Video series’ upcoming third season. The massive production has taken over a large section of Windsor Great Park, which has been used as an outdoor setting for numerous films in the past, including Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows and The Huntsman: Winter’s War.

It’s a gargantuan setup, with dozens of vehicles, tents and trailers nearby, along with a small army of actors in full Orc and Elvish regalia. And it happens to be just one aspect of a massive logistical puzzle that has to happen to make the show possible. “It's a [huge] production every time we do this. We have four units running right now, including ours,” notes McKay. “One unit is over in a place called Frensham (about 25 miles south of Windsor), shooting [a scene] with the dwarf characters. Then we have another unit that is shooting various sundry action sequences back at Shepperton Studios, and a fourth unit is prepping [scenes] we will be shooting in a few weeks.”

When it returns for its third season on November 11 , Rings of Power will be making a significant time jump in the storyline. Season 3 will be set five years after the events of Season 2 , when Sauron did away with his disguise and sent the Elves into retreat as his armies overran Middle-earth. McKay embraced making such a pronounced jump in the narrative timeline, because it drops the viewer right in the center of the action, making them catch up to the story.

“We really love the idea of throwing the viewer in in a way that is a completely fresh start. J.D. Payne, my co-showrunner and I, we're huge admirers of shows that have done this kind of [time jump] before, like Battlestar Galactica and Halt and Catch Fire,” he says. “That can be really fun for a viewer.”

According to McKay, it’s also an opportunity to do a soft reboot and send the series in a new direction. “Hopefully, this season is a great jumping-on point for fans,” he says. “And it truly starts with people talking about the One Ring.”

He admits that filming the first two seasons back to back was an enormous strain on everyone involved, and believes the upcoming season will benefit from having more breathing room. “I think our goal for Season 3 is really to blow the doors off the hinges,” McKay says. “We're really proud of Seasons One and Two, but …for us, now, in some ways, we're starting a whole new story. This is turning the page on the show.”

The showrunners have already benefited from the fact that their series is not based on a detailed narrative like The Fellowship of the Ring or The Hobbit . While it’s a prequel to the LOTR stories set in the Second Age of Middle-earth, Rings of Power is not a direct adaptation of any single Tolkien work; instead it draws mainly on Tolkien’s background lore and appendices for inspiration. That has allowed the show’s creatives to forge their own path. Tolkien himself, in a correspondence published in The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, said this era in Middle-earth was a dark age, where “not very much of its history is (or need be) told. “

“There's lots of room for original characters in this era of the mythology,” McKay says about the breathing room the creative team has for the series. “Tolkien gave us a very broad outline … an outline that sometimes contradicts itself depending on where you're reading.”

McKay and Payne enjoy a fairly wide berth with which to craft the story that drives the series. They’ve introduced several new concepts and characters, one of the most notable being Adar, an integral figure in the first two seasons of Rings of Power. Adar was an Elf who was corrupted and twisted by Morgoth into being one of the first Orcs. He viewed the Orcs as his children, and they viewed him as their Lord-father. He was ultimately betrayed and killed by a band of Orcs loyal to Sauron in the Season 2 finale , Shadow and Flame.

Delivering a new character like Adar into Middle-earth involves a certain process which involves discussions with Tolkien scholar Carl F. Hostetter, who serves as a linguist and consultant on the series. “Usually we change the name to fit more the conventions of how he used his accenting and the types of sounds he would use and everything else,” McKay says. “We're inventing in, hopefully, a way that is really informed.”

The presentation of the Orcs is one of the most notable detours the series takes from Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings movies . In the films, the Orcs are mainly a collective of terror and brute force. By that time period in the Rings mythos, they have devolved into an existence of serving as Sauron’s blunt instruments of war and destruction.

In Rings of Power, Orcs are not simply rampaging monsters. They are more complex, with distinct personalities and deeply personal motivations. Fans even got a glimpse of an Orc family last season when we met the Orc Glûg, his wife and child. Of course, Sauron viciously kills Glûg to sow distrust among the other Orcs and turn them against Adar. But that tragic ending underscores how in the Second Age, the Orcs are more than just mindless cannon fodder.

The expansion of the Orcs as a more complicated aspect of Middle-earth continues in Season 3 as we are introduced to the character of Marnouk , an Orc unlike any we’ve ever seen in a Tolkien adaptation. He appears in Rivendell claiming to be a defector from Sauron’s army who wants to help the Elves fight back. “He claims to know all kinds of things about Sauron's strategy and reveals to the Elves that Sauron is trying to make the One Ring ,” says McKay. “And if he succeeds, he will defeat everyone, including the Orcs, because the One Ring will now make them subservient to him, slaves to him forever, and there'll never be another Orc rebellion like Adar, who died last season, led.”

Marnouk is a character meant to challenge long-held perceptions of Orcs. He’s such a departure from past depictions that within the production, Marnouk has picked up the catchy nickname, “the Orc with an arc.”

IGN was the only media outlet on set for the filming of key moments of an episode in Season 3 where Marnouk is being escorted by Galadriel and Arondir. There is a tension and uncertainty hovering above the trio’s interactions, notes the episode’s director, Sanaa Hamri, that viewers won’t know how to feel about him at first.

"I have a real soft spot for this Orc," admits Hamri. "I think the audience is going to be really torn about Marnouk."

Adam Young , the actor who portrays the new Orc, says having the audience question Marnouk’s true purpose is a central element of his performance. “We were working out early on what was his incentive? What's his purpose for being here? Is he good, is he bad?,” Young notes.

During the scenes I witnessed, there is noticeable tension as Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and especially Arondir (Ismael Cruz Cordova) are suspicious of their travel companion, who claims to know the location of the one remaining element Sauron needs to create the One Ring. That unease is heightened by certain moments, such as the one I saw filmed. It’s a sequence where the group comes across a field littered with the corpses of Elves. Marnouk urges the Elves to take a detour, a suggestion that is met with understandable suspicion. There are also moments of levity that add a new layer to the complex relationship between the three; Arondir, besides being wary of Marnouk, is visibly annoyed by the Orc’s constant chatter.

“He's a wizard with words. He's a word spiller,” Young says. “It's just been really fun to play around with him and come and join Miv and Ismael on that journey and come into the family.”

The trio seem like an intentional callback to another unlikely group of travelers from Rings lore. “It's a little bit like Frodo, Sam and Gollum,” McKay admits. “Galadriel had this very grudging respect that developed between her and Adar so she's maybe a little more willing to maybe believe there's something to what Marnouk is saying.”

But while Galadriel may be willing to give the Orc a chance to prove himself, her Elven partner is not. “Arondir's interactions with Orcs have been terrible. They basically killed the woman he loved,” McKay points out. “So he's like, ‘I don't believe him. I think it's a lie.’ And so you've got this dynamic from the three of them where the audience will constantly not be sure that they can trust this guy. Is he out for himself? Is he working on Sauron's [behalf]? And that becomes a journey of a big part of the season, and there's quite a few twists and turns along the way.”

The misdirection Marnouk’s character conveys at different points meant the show’s prosthetics department, led by multiple Emmy Award winner Barry Gower, had their work cut out for them.

“We knew he was going to have an awful lot of dialogue and there was going to be a lot of exposure to his face, so he would need to convey a lot of emotion [through his facial expressions],” notes Gower. “It dictated how we designed his prosthetics.”

Gower is no stranger to massive productions, having worked on blockbuster series like Game of Thrones , Stranger Things , and The Last of Us . Rings of Power has posed its own unique challenges with regards to the sheer number of different prosthetic designs used onscreen. Gower’s crew has amassed a trove of Orc character designs since Rings debuted. In fact, for the epic Siege of Eregion that served as the climactic battle to the second season , nearly 1,700 different Orc makeup designs were created. And if you’re wondering how they can possibly not repeat themselves while having to create so many Orc looks, well … Gower and his team had the same concern.

So after production wrapped on Season 2, they created a library of different Orc designs, featuring character designs as well as a variety of details such as different types of hair, contact lenses and dentures. That way they can cobble together different looks depending on the needs of the storyline.

“So Season 2 we didn't have that catalog to start off with. We started from the ground upwards and we did a lot of concept art and design and did some three-dimensional sculptures to distinguish these characters,” Gower says. “This time we've got this catalog and we can go to the showrunners and say, ‘What about this guy from last year, something on a variation of this with a little bit of this?’ So, it's actually really lovely that we've got all this.”

The type of material used for Orc prosthetics on Rings of Power varies by necessity. Due to the sheer number of Orc characters who show up during a big battle sequence, i.e. stunt actors and background players, the prosthetics are often an assembly of foam latex pieces from 10 to 15 different Orc designs. “We can take the forehead from one and put it with the cheeks of another and the nose of one and mix and match them as such, like a jigsaw puzzle,” says Gower.

For Marnouk, Gower and his crew had to create an entirely new design to accommodate his performance. It began with a 3D scan of the actor, which was then used to create a clay maquette of the character. That maquette is then used as the blueprint to sculpt the full-scale makeup.

“With somebody like Adam, it's a bespoke make-up, made particularly for Adam Young,” he says. “And it's made out of a silicon gel material. Very, very flexible, very, very soft. But we actually sculpted and made the application very thin.”

“So even though he's got a big Orc-like nose and big Orc ears and he's got an Orc chin, what have you, we've made sure that the forehead in particular and the cheeks were very thin and could give Adam a lot of movement,” Gower adds. “So everything that he did with his performance would show through the application, basically.”

There is a brief but key moment in the scene I saw being filmed where Marnouk tells his escorts/captors, “I give you my word” as he tries to convince them he’s telling the truth about the path he wants to take. It’s a close-up shot, and the emotion in the delivery is amplified by the incredible detail in Young’s prosthetics makeup. The whites of Young’s eyes stand out surrounded by the green of the Orc prosthetics, and the exposed bone and scars complement the look. I should note that Young has crystal-blue eyes in real life, so he also has to wear contact lenses to complete his Orc look.

“He’s very emotive, so in a way it really is like a second skin for him,” Gower says. “But it was just really important chatting with the showrunners that he was able to convey as wide a range of emotions as possible because he looks really sinister and evil in some points, And he looks very surprised and very joyful in some shots as well. We just had to make sure that Adam was never going to be fighting the make-up to convey his performance.”

I talked with Young in-between takes while he was in full makeup, in the supply center section of the production the crew affectionately call ‘Orc-ia.’. Getting used to the prosthetics and figuring out how to convey certain expressions without overdoing it took some time. “It's been a lot of me in the mirror looking at myself every day and figuring it all out,” Young says. “I mean, I was pretty blown away by how much movement and emotion I could get out of it by not actually doing a lot. And once I get the teeth in, once I get the lenses in, it's great.”

The London-based actor, whose credits include The Witcher: Blood Origin , Masters of the Air , and EastEnders, recalls getting the news that he’d landed the role during the Christmas holiday. He then immediately began immersing himself in Rings lore, which he admits he was not that familiar with.

“I’d actually never read the books and so I just [threw] myself into the Tolkien world and Silmarillion and all of that,” Young says. “It was really nice to just have a bit of time to actually jump into that and the language and the lore. It's huge.”

It didn’t take long for the actor to notice the parallels between his character stepping into the story and Young’s arrival on a show where much of the cast and crew have been together for several years.

“I was just saying to [my publicist] the other day that me as Adam coming into the Rings family and me as the character coming into that narrative was a … similar thing, in my head,” he says. “It felt quite distant at first, and then I got to know everyone.”

Young is well aware of the plum opportunity he has, coming into a beloved franchise like Lord of the Rings and getting to portray a different side of a character that has often been one-dimensional. He says the questions the audience will have about Marnouk when Season 3 debuts are the same ones he had to figure out when he landed the role.

“Is he good, is he bad? Do we know? Is he smarter than he makes out? And what's his drive? He's coming out of Sauron's world … I don't want to say too much on that, but what's his purpose?,” says Young. “That's been a lot of fun to play around with. And for the audience, it’s working out whether they trust him. And they will see as the show goes on, he's a tough nut to crack.”

articles.title: Ratata, A 4-Player Physics-Chaos Co-op Game Where You Play as Anthropomorphic Animals, Announced
articles.summary: Introducing Ratata, a chaotic four-player co-op physics game where you and three friends play as a gang of animals who owe money to a mafia toad. Choose your animal – complete with its own unique strengths and weaknesses that are best suited to each mission – and then build your garage, get the thing the boss wants, pack the truck, deliver the goods, and do it all while dressed like you're in an '80s crime heist movie.
articles.body:
Introducing Ratata, a chaotic four-player co-op physics game where you and three friends play as a gang of animals who owe money to a mafia toad. Choose your animal – complete with its own unique strengths and weaknesses that are best suited to each mission – and then build your garage, get the thing the boss wants, pack the truck, deliver the goods, and do it all while dressed like you're in an '80s crime heist movie.

Ratata is being developed by The Kingsdom, and it's in the works for PC. It can be played solo or with up to four players total, and as you can see from the announcement trailer above and the first screenshots in the gallery below, it's got a very cartoony, fun art style. It aims to match that on the gameplay side, with physics-based chaos making every job an unpredictable mess (in the best of ways).

Choose your animal carefully, as The Kingsdom says, "every animal has its own size, strength, speed, abilities and driver's license status. One animal can be perfect for one job and a disaster for the next." Hazards include having to "sneak past guards, dodge traps and outrun crazy granny squirrels."

Ratata doesn't have a release date as of yet, but you can wishlist it on Steam if you're interested.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.summary: What did Steve Kerr have to say about the unusual WNBA Finals Game 6 start time?
articles.body:
The Golden State Valkyries got a massive 64-55 Game 5 victory over the Atlanta Dream in the WNBA Finals. Valkyries center Kiah Stokes was a game-changer. She dropped 13 points, hit multiple three-pointers, and had three blocks.

articles.title: This insane stat shows how patient Brewers' offense has been in World Series
articles.summary: Stats like this explain why the Brewers have been so good in this World Series.
articles.body:
Game 3 of the 2026 World Series was a complete and total blowout win for the Milwaukee Brewers . It ended 10-1, and now the Brewers just one more win over the Tampa Bay Rays from winning their franchise's first-ever title.

There are plenty of wild statistics behind the Brewers' dominance in this World Series, from individual players like Jackson Chourio, Jacob Misiorowski, and Robert Gasser. But as a team, the Brewers accomplished something Monday that is hard to believe.

ESPN's Buster Olney shared an insane statistic that shows just how patient the Brewers' offense has been in Game 3 of the World Series. On 130 pitches seen by Brewers' hitters, only 12 resulted in a swing and a miss.

Insane Brewers stat shows just how impressive this offense has been

"The Brewers have just 12 missed swings among the 130 pitches they've seen," Olney shared on Twitter/x.

This is one of those statistics that's hard to believe, but it tells the whole story of how Game 3 went for the Brewers' hitters and Rays' pitchers.

That statistic was shared partway through the game, and the Rays threw another 45 pitches over the final three innings against Brewers hitters.

Across the final three innings, the 45 pitches Brewers' hitters saw resulted in just three more swings and misses. So, that brings the final total of swings and misses from Brewers hitters in the third game of the World Series to just 15.

On 175 pitches seen in this game, Brewers hitters swung and missed at a pitch just 15 times. Brewers hitters only swung and missed at a pitch every 11.6 pitches in this game, good for roughly a ridiculous 8.57% swing-and-miss rate.

This is the kind of performance that's agonizing for opposing pitchers, as they clearly were struggling to put away hitters all night.

Now, one game from baseball immortality, the Brewers are acting as patient as ever, and it's leading to immense offensive success.

This Brewers offense is just as patient as the fans have been waiting to see this team win a World Series. That patience is paying off, both for the fan base eagerly awaiting one more win and the Brewers' lineup that's so close to a World Series championship.

articles.title: The Brewers' good-luck charm this postseason has been...an announcer?
articles.summary: Josh Maurer is calling one inning a game this postseason. More often than not, those have been memorable for the Brewers.
articles.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, FL — Josh Maurer had no way of knowing what would be ahead of him, but first he just needed to understand what the text message from fellow Milwaukee Brewers broadcaster Jeff Levering was even saying.

"You have the fifth," Levering texted Maurer the morning of Game 1 of the National League Division Series.

Maurer looked at it for a minute. "The fifth inning?" he replied.

And with that, Maurer was thrust into the radio play-by-play seat for some of the most memorable moments of the greatest October run the Brewers franchise has ever seen.

In Game 4 of the NLDS, Maurer called the go-ahead and eventual game-winning run. In Game 1 of the National League Championship Series, the same thing happened. In Game 2, William Contreras hit a game-tying homer. In Game 4, the Brewers clawed back to tie it again with two more runs.

And then Game 3 of the World Series happened. As the Brewers offense went berserk with eight two-out runs that will live on for years, it was Maurer on the call.

In the immediate aftermath of the call, Maurer was still taken aback.

"The word that keeps coming to my mind is fortunate," he said. "I'm just so fortunate. I shouldn't even be in this position to be broadcasting, and because Lane [Grindle] and Jeff have been so gracious I am. To be able to narrate that inning is the honor of my career."

It all happened fast. From Brice Turang's two-run single to kick off the scoring until Jackson Chourio's double to cap it was 10 minutes.

"Tonight's was actually easy," he said. "I thought it was easier because what was happening was just all these hits. There wasn't anything complicated about it. Just constant chaos. When things are drawn out it makes it harder, but when it's like that you don't have time to get creative. You just keep going."

This is the first MLB postseason that Maurer has ever called. He's been with the club since 2022, but his first two years that Milwaukee made the postseason the call was split by Levering, Grindle and Bob Uecker. Last year, Levering and Grindle handled the games.

This year, they wanted Maurer to join, making for a full-circle moment. The last time Maurer called a playoff game was 2014 in the minor leagues with Levering. Before Game 1 of the World Series, the two took a moment to acknowledge how far they've come.

In this case, that meant calling one of the biggest innings in Brewers history.

Brewers fans roll out superstitions ahead of Game 3 watch party

"It really hit me right away," Maurer said. "From the minute Turang got that hit and [Garrett] Mitchell got another one and then right after that it was [Cooper] Pratt, it was three pitches. They scored five runs on three pitches. That was when I was like, 'Oh, my God, I can't believe how lucky I am.' That's really what I was thinking: 'I can't believe this is happening while I'm calling play-by-play.

articles.title: Wandering Cat's Cage Is a Dystopian Manga Worth Reading
articles.summary: We've got an exclusive preview of Wandering Cat's Cage, a haunting new dystopian manga from Fantagraphics and MSX: Mangasplaining Extra.
articles.body:
Fantagraphics new East Asian-focused manga imprint Takumigraphics has been a gold mine for manga lovers, and that trend looks to continue with their latest release. Next up is Wandering Cat's Cage, a dystopian shojo manga from Akane Torikai (Sensei’s Pious Lie).

With Wandering Cat's Cage in stores today, IGN can exclusively reveal a new preview of the manga. Check it out in the slideshow gallery below:

Wandering Cat's Cage is published in collaboration between Fantagraphics and MSX: Mangasplaining Extra. Here's the official summary of the new book:

Master manga-ka Akane Torikai’s Wandering Cat’s Cage takes place in a near-future, where only a few women are still able to menstruate, and even fewer men will be born to them.Reproduction is limited to medical intervention controlled from on high, and the structures and lives of the past are only hinted at through scraps of a world that no longer exists. Life can be good, though, if you fall in line. The women of The City live bright, happy, tightly controlled lives. But complete obedience isn’t for everyone. For the women across the river, who live in a rundown shantytown, life is different. It is humble, and often dangerous, but it is free.

Sanada, a young acupuncturist, lives across the river with the mysterious Reiho, the only male she’s ever met who sells himself to the rich women who sneak across the river for something they’ve never experienced. The two form a small “family,” taking in other young women ousted from the city. But when Reiho is kidnapped at gunpoint and taken to the breeding program in The City, Sanada must join the other outcasts to rescue him and learn the difficult truths of love, self-actualization, society, safety, and humanity’s future.

“Akane Torikai's Wandering Cat's Cage is a perfect addition to the Takumigraphics line,” said Fantagraphics’ Vice President and Associate Publisher Eric Reynolds in a press release. “Building on traditions of shojo manga and dystopian fiction pioneered by artists like Moto Hagio and Katsuhiro Otomo, Torikai advances both genres with her gorgeous artwork in the service of an urgent and fierce voice for our current time.”

Wandering Cat's Cage is available in bookstores now. You can order a copy on Amazon .

articles.title: South Korean Politician Urges President to Play Modern Warfare 4 to Understand 'Devastation' of Potential Invasion
articles.summary: A South Korean politician has urged the country's President to play Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to grasp the potential devastation from a North Korean invasion.
articles.body:
A South Korean politician has urged the country's President to play Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to grasp the potential devastation of a North Korean invasion.

In a report from Korean outlet The Herald Business , politician Han Dong-hoon urged President Lee Jae-myung to play Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to grasp how catastrophic things could be if the country was ill-equipped to defend against a North Korean invasion. He noted that the country should be actively preparing for any kind of situation, rather than simply hoping it never happens. He also pushed back against critiques of the game depicting an active all-out war between the two countries, believing that it should be a wake-up call to assess whether or not they're prepared for something like that to happen.

"I hope the image of a Seoul reduced to ashes in the game remains in the realm of fiction," he said.

In Modern Warfare 4, the game opens with a group of South Korean soldiers patrolling the city streets before an EMP takes out all power in the area. The North Korean army then attacks the city with a barrage of missiles before air-dropping soldiers and launching offensive measures through a series of tunnels. It's pure chaos, not unlike the surprise Russian invasion of America in the original Modern Warfare 2 from 2009.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Campaign Screenshots

Half of Modern Warfare 4's story focuses on South Korean forces trying to push the North Korean opposition back, despite being hopelessly outmatched and overpowered, partially thanks to a groundbreaking new technology that can wipe out defenses in the blink of an eye. The story also feels oddly timed, as reports last week claimed that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un had fallen into a coma or even outright died .

These reports have been denied and countered, but the comparison to the game came as Kim Jong Un's sister, Kim Yo Jong, made threats against South Korea . In Modern Warfare 4, there's a familial power struggle within North Korean leadership, which ends with the Supreme Leader's sister taking command and unleashing war on South Korea. Given the timing of the real-life situation and the release of Modern Warfare 4 last week, it was hard for fans not to see eerie similarities between reality and the game's fictional story.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 also has an entire mode set in the DMZ , a real-world location that sits on the border of North and South Korea. In the game, the player explores this environment to complete missions, extract loot, and learn additional lore about the game's story. IGN gave Modern Warfare 4 a 7/10 , noting that the game's multiplayer feels a bit too familiar, but the campaign elevates the larger package: "Multiplayer may not quite hit the mark, but a great campaign ensures Modern Warfare 4's place as one of Call of Duty’s better recent entries," reads an excerpt from our review.

articles.title: Blizzard Teases Familiar Locations for Post-Launch World of Warcraft Forever Updates
articles.summary: World of Warcraft Forever gets its full release on November 4, and while the MMO will stay tethered to the two vanilla continents, Eastern Kingdoms and Kalimdor, it sounds like future updates could add some of the areas we've visited in the expansions.
articles.body:
World of Warcraft Forever gets its full release on November 4, and while the MMO will stay tethered to the two vanilla continents, Eastern Kingdoms and Kalimdor, it sounds like future updates could add some of the areas we've visited in the expansions.

I recently got a chance to sit down with Blizzard principal game designer Kris Zierhut to talk about the future of WoW Forever, and when I asked him if there were threads the developer could pull at to find new content "without going to outer space," Zierhut responded by saying: "Correct, correct. Now, that said, the Dark Portal exists, Northrend exists, Pandaria exists, and we could make minor forays into those areas. We might have a dungeon or a quest that takes you there for a mission or two and come back."

So, rather than going to these places for these multi-year epic quests, like going to Northrend to stop Arthas, it seems like these would be little jaunts to a different part of the world, then quickly returning back to the vanilla continents.

Zierhut emphasized that any journeys to other parts of Azeroth would be brief, saying: "But the key detail there is Eastern Kingdoms and Kalimdor are your home. You don't have capital cities, you don't have auction houses and innkeepers and things like that outside of Eastern Kingdom and Kalimdor. We won't introduce new capital cities in this plan. Okay. You always come home."

Later on in the interview, Zierhut clarified that the versions of these continents wouldn't be the same as what we've visited in the expansions. Using Northrend as an example, he told me: "If we ever went to Northrend, we wouldn't be visiting the version that you see in Wrath of the Lich King . But could we visit some extremely hostile level 60 version of it because Arthas is still in the stage where he's sending Kel’Thuzad to Eastern Kingdoms to assault Eastern Plaguelands? We could. There's so much that we can do with the timeline that we're in."

While it seems like working in areas from the expansions would run counter to Forever's mission statement, the developers are more focused on maintaining the spirit of classic WoW, rather than strictly adhering to the same content that we played in 2004 and 2019. For instance, Blizzard took a pretty early stance against adding features like group tagging , because it wanted players to group up and do content together. But, later on, it added the 'Kyle's Gone Missing' quest, even though it intially came out as a part of The Burning Crusade , because it fit with the spirit of the original game.

Forever is also adding entirely new parts of the world, including some maps, like Mount Hyjal, that were originally supposed to be part of the original World of Warcraft, but didn't make the final cut. It's going to be interesting to see what direction future content is going to go in, because unlike other versions of Classic, Blizzard doesn't have to rigidly stick to what World of Warcraft did in the past. One thing's for sure, though, we won't have to wait as long between patches as some of the older WoW expansions .

articles.title: Blizzard Reveals Plan for World of Warcraft Forever Update Frequency
articles.summary: World of Warcraft Forever launches a week from today, and while the game will have a huge swath of content available on day one, there will be new content continually added to the game. But how frequently should fans expect new content to arrive? It sounds like Blizzard is willing to take things a little slower than in the modern version of World of Warcraft.
articles.body:
World of Warcraft Forever launches a week from today, and while the game will have a huge swath of content available on day one, there will be new content continually added to the game. But how frequently should fans expect new content to arrive? It sounds like Blizzard is willing to take things a little slower than in the modern version of World of Warcraft.

In a recent interview with IGN , World of Warcraft Forever principal game designer Kris Zierhut, said Forever will employ a slower cadence than Midnight's aggressive eight-week content cycle: "We're fairly convinced the correct [update] rate is something closer to once every four months or 17 weeks or three times a year."

This is in contrast with the modern version of World of Warcraft, which has had an aggressive update cadence since Dragonflight launched in 2022. And while that approach has meant players of the modern version of the game have something new every couple of months, some have said the updates often feels rushed, with bugs and repeated content. We've all done some form of invasions several times in the last couple of years, after all.

Zierhut did say that Blizzard experimented with a faster update schedule in Season of Discovery, an experimental Classic game mode that came out in 2023, but "we cut it down to closer to that eight week or 10 week schedule. It felt way, way, way too fast."

But by going with a four month update schedule, Forever will also avoid the content droughts that some older expansions were infamous for. There have been times in WoW's history where the game didn't have new content for a year at a time, like in Warlords of Draenor, where patch 6.2, which included Hellfire Citadel, lasted for 13 months before the prepatch update for Legion.

Zierhut acknowledged this as well, saying: "We've played around with different rates of releasing content and going six or eight months without new stuff always feels bad. We know that."

Just because World of Warcraft patches will be released in four-month intervals, it doesn't necessarily mean you'll have to wait four months for something new to do. Zierhut also told me that the team may timegate some content, saying "one nuance on that is we do plan on making content that unlocks in between. So you might have patches with major releases four months apart, but there may be things that unlock two or three months in or one month into that."

The idea there is to ease players into content, rather than overwhelming them with everything all at once. Zierhut continued: "It's not just patch day comes [around], here's a content fire hose, and now we're silent for four months. A lot of that is, 'hey, there's a time event calendar that gradually unlocks things and opens them up over those four months' to give things a little bit more life instead of that all at once effect."

Only time will tell if this middle ground between rapid updates and slow updates will pay off, but according to the roadmap that Blizzard released at BlizzCon, Forever will have its first major update sometime in spring 2027. So, if that four-month timeline that Blizzard is targeting pays off, WoW Forever should have a fresh round of new content sometime in March.

While you wait for the game to launch, check out more on Blizzard's plan for World of Warcraft Forever .

articles.body:
Now that the World of Warcraft Forever beta has come to an end, Blizzards alternative history version of Vanilla WoW is finally ready for a full launch on November 4. But even though the beta was extensive, it was capped at level 30, which leaves plenty of mystery for fans. Luckily I was able to sit down with Blizzard principal game designer Kris Zierhut and lead Classic designer Tim Jones to tour through the game and chat about what the future holds. And, really, it does sound like WoW Forever is going to take a pretty unique path as it unfolds over the next few years.

Kris Zierhut: I know you're very interested in this question of what it means to have a single subscription with these three pillars that we talked about at BlizzCon and how they're different and what each of them means. We should probably start with WoW Classic, because it’s kind of the base start. Take somewhere like Elwynn Forest where you're going to go to. It's been that zone for 22 years with very little change, and Classic Era, the Classic cycle, really the Burning Crusade, Wrath of the Lich King as well, is really when we think of it a little bit like a museum. It's what the game was, so we can preserve that forever for the people who loved it and for reference and people to see, oh, what was it like back then? So it's an attempt to just recreate the world as it was in that 2004 to 2008 cycle.

And now Forever is saying, well, what if instead of opening the Dark Portal and moving on to Outland, what if that dev team back in 2006, Jeff Kaplan and Tom Chilton and Scott Mercer and Eric Dodds and me, other people on the team, what if we'd stayed in the original world and kept on developing it and done things that were consistent with what they would've done back then?

Whether that's adding additional quests... So here in Elwynn, there's one major new quest line that involves Kobolds stealing books. But every start area has new quests, every zone has new quests, new things to discover. We've made a great effort to look at all of the rare creatures in the world and make sure each of them has unique and interesting things that they drop if you fight the rare creatures.

Or things like Trade Skills, where we made Trade Skills more prominent, achieved Eric Dodds' original vision for what Trades could be by adding to them, adding new recipes and making it more important and more balanced with the rest of the game. So if they've been able to work on the game for a couple more years before releasing it, what would they have done? And then of course, modern.

IGN: How did Blizzard decide on what stayed from Classic unchanged, then what was added that was probably more of a modern feature? Because I know the DPS meters and the Cooldown Manager are in Forever.

Zierhut: Right. First, we look at our four major pillars on our design values. Way back when we were starting to make changes in Wrath of the Lich King Classic, you said, "Hey, before we get started on this whole path of making changes, what is important to us? What are our guiding principles of making the world still feel classic?" The most important probably of those is ‘the world is the main character.’ We think the world has a story that you discover while you explore it with your friends. It's your player stories when you wander into these quirky little places that have their own local stories about minor characters and not world shattering events and not major NPCs.

It's about the journey being just as important as the destination, that there's all kinds of cool things to discover and experience along the way, and we want to make sure that we keep adding new things to see along the way. It's not all about max level.

And I think that's probably one of the biggest philosophical differences between retail as you call it, and what Forever is. Retail is very focused on what's going on at max level. We create a new campaign, you level up through the campaign and now you're max level again. And it's all about things for max level, where we want to keep on delivering new things to do all the way through the level up experience and reasons to make new characters and experience the journey all over again.

A sort of goal of that is then to make sure that the world always feels full, no matter what zone you go to, there's always characters in that level range. We were very inspired by World of Warcraft Hardcore in that. We loved how in Hardcore it always felt like every zone you went to was full of other players. It was never empty, and part of that was because you always had to re-roll a new character when you died. We were looking for how we could get the same kind of effect in World of Warcraft Forever by encouraging [players] to make new characters and experience the journey again.

Approachable and familiar, which is an interesting pillar because in some ways. It's a little bit at war with itself. We want the game to be approachable in the sense that we want a new player, somebody who's never played World of Warcraft, to walk up in 2026. And by the way, we know there are many, many tens of thousands of people in this category just from seeing in the beta.

A new player who's never played before, can they learn the game and find it approachable and understand it and become new people to go on the journey? Can we continue to grow and collect new players? So, [being] approachable is very important. And the original classic game was very, very approachable. And then familiar is, well, as much as possible, try to keep things familiar to what was in the Classic era. So if you played in the Classic era and you come into Forever, you're like, oh yeah, this feels like how that used to work. This feels familiar to me. I'm home. I'm not in some alien, strange place.

And a lot of that was careful attention to things like the models, where we decided we wanted to keep the standard definition models or at least an option between standard definition and high definition models and the animations on them. The way we decided to go about the lighting and shadows of the world and making sure that things felt the same as they always had, or the UI, making sure that while we're using a lot of modern UI conveniences you talked about, that it still feels like a classic game and not just a copy of the Retail UI. It feels like its own game with its own UI goals.

And finally, our last big pillar was to nurture and protect social experiences. So we feel that one of the Classic era's biggest strengths was just how social a game it was. You need other people to do things, to make progress on the big things. Now, you could go adventure by yourself, you can make progress by yourself, but the game's just kind of always better with friends to do a dungeon, to do a harder quest, to do a raid. There's always opportunities to have friends and get more out of the game.

So for that, we leaned into new systems like the new camping system, which is designed to help people have good experiences. They run into each other in the wilderness. I find somebody out in the wilds in Feralas and they've got a camp and I sit down at camp and I add something to it. They're happy, I'm happy. We both get buffs. We have to sit there for a minute and talk to each other. And when we talk to each it's like, 'Hey, we're working on the same quest.'

Well, let's group up and do it together. It'll be faster. It'll be easier. We log in the next day and say, oh, that person's on my ‘recently played with’ list. Maybe I'll ask them to play with me again. Maybe they still have some quest in Feralas. And soon an actual relationship is born that continues past those couple encounters.

That's our goal, our vision for how that works. And so those pillars drive a lot of our decision making. So we say, 'Hey, we want to change this thing. I've got this idea for how I could change it. Should we do it or not?' Well, does it strengthen those pillars? Does it weaken those pillars? Does it do something sort of neutral? And we try to pick only the things that strengthen the pillars.

One area we made a lot of changes on is sort of a sub-goal that we ran across during development, which is the idea of ‘unsolving’ the game. People who've been playing Classic era for the last 21, 22 years, they know the perfect leveling path. They know exactly what Trade Skills to take, exactly what talents to take, exactly what gear to collect. And we wanted to make a new experience so somebody familiar with how it played before understands how it works, but maybe what they've done 10 or more times before isn't always the right choice.

IGN: One of the biggest questions I've had about Forever since it was announced at BlizzCon is, there's all these graphics improvements, and the game looks incredible, especially when it comes to lighting and the water physics. Why were these improvements made here and not in the modern version of the game?

Zierhut: I think they were made here first, is a better clarification. I think they're planning on eventually doing some of these same things in the Retail game as well. So it's not like it's a Forever-only feature, like better water, better lighting, those things are coming for retail as well. I don't know when, but I know they're talking about doing it.

But why here? A few reasons. One big one is in our minds 20 years later, we remember what WoW was like in 2004 as just a little bit shinier and better than it actually was. So there's this vision of, let's give people Azeroth as they remember it, not as it actually was. They remember it having spectacular graphics and these crazy vistas and lighting and shadows, but when you go back and look at it and say, oh yeah, we've made a lot of progress making these things better. This isn't as great anymore as it used to be, but I remember it being that great. So let's make it actually look as cool as our memories tell us it looked. That was one part of driving it.

Another part of driving it was those tens of thousands of new players we're talking about. We want to bring in the next generation of gamers who are used to a lot of these higher graphical fidelity things. Let's bring that into Forever, especially if we can maintain World of Warcraft's classic style and visual aesthetic, which we did. I think we did an excellent job. The game looks like the same game in terms of the style, the art style and the types of characters and the types of buildings you see, but it just looks so much more beautiful than it did before.

IGN: How much of a lift was it bringing these new graphic systems to the WoW engine? Because I know the WoW engine is famously huge and I’ve heard the word spaghetti code a few times in the forums, for instance.

Zierhut: It is not spaghetti code. I think that's totally an unfair player characterization. I think it's personally one of the best game engines out there. When I have friends go off to, because they've left Blizzard to work in another company, work in other engines, when we have conversations like, 'Oh man, I wish I just had the WoW engine. Could we just license the WoW engine? It would be so much easier, better to do the things I want to do.' I've heard that comment repeatedly from other developers.

And kind of the opposite of spaghetti code. What our developers have done over the last really 25 years, because it started even before the game came out, was continually improve the engine and make updates to make it run better, run more efficiently. We can get a higher frame rate, have more units in the same area, [and] have better server response times because we've been perfecting these algorithms and making them better and better and better every year.

And now it's really hard to catch up. It's the best that there is because it's been continuously developed for 25 years, which is the complete opposite of spaghetti code. It's really a fantastic engine. Players say that on the forums and it really isn't that. There's bugs, that's what players say when there's bugs. And any piece of software is going to have bugs. That's reality.

World of Warcraft: Midnight Cinematic Images and First Screenshots

IGN: On the subject of bugs, another thing I've been curious about is what the update schedule for this game is going to look like. Because one of the biggest topics in the modern version of the game right now is the eight week patch cadence since Dragonflight. I've seen a lot of people complaining about repeated content and buggy launches. Are the future updates for Forever going to be coming as frequently or is it just going to be more laid back, slow growth?

Zierhut: I’d say it's a little more laid back. What we've identified through a lot of experimentation, everybody on the dev team, not only are we super involved in designing this game, but we've all been playing the Classic era games continuously since [they] came out in 2019. And we've played around with different rates of releasing content, and going six or eight months without new stuff always feels bad. We know that.

But Season of Discovery, we cut it down to closer to that eight week or 10 week schedule. It felt way, way, way too fast. So we've done a lot of experimentation to see what is the correct rate, and we're fairly convinced the correct rate is something closer to once every four months or 17 weeks or three times a year, whatever you want to call it. That is a cadence we have in mind for releasing new content.

And our plan for being able to do that is essentially, we say we have this much time, how much can we fit in the time? That's one of the advantages of telling smaller stories and more localized stories, is we don't have a giant huge story that needs six months to be told.

We come up with enough local stories that it's appropriate for a four month development period and then we release that four months and then we can have dangling threads to the story that we finish later. But the cadence intent is about four months, at least between raid tiers is four months. Our plan for PVP seasons, and there will be PVP seasons, is four months between seasons. So it's a little more laid back than Retail, but not as laid back as some Classic era expansions, where you might go six months or longer between new raid tiers and new things to do.

And then one nuance on that is we do plan on making content that unlocks in between. So you might have patches with major releases four months apart, but there may be things that unlock two or three months in or one month into that.

So you want to stagger out some content across those four months. It's not just patch day comes [around], here's a content fire hose, and now we're silent for four months. A lot of that is, hey, there's a time event calendar that gradually unlocks things and opens them up over those four months to give things a little bit more life instead of that all at once effect. And Tim's actually the wizard of doing all that stuff.

IGN: So I know that thematically we're talking about just living within Azeroth and not having these giant universe ending threats. When there are updates, is it going to follow the same path that Vanilla did when it was first coming out? Are we going to Molten Core? Are we going to Naxxramus? Or is it going to be a new path?

Zierhut: There's going to be a new path and old path. At BlizzCon, Josh talked about, there's three types of content we want to add to the game. They're the things that you expect the classic era had. Molten Core, Blackwing Lair, An’Qiraj. We will go to those places. We'll go through it a little slower. We're not starting with Molten Core. We're kind of slowing down the timeline and stretching it out a bit, but we will go to those places you expect.

And then there are places that are new but feel like they do belong. So we're going to go to... we added the Riverglades zone and we added a new dungeon there that's an ogre dungeon. And those didn't exist, but they feel appropriate. And as we add new places, new raids and dungeons, there'll be some in that category as well. They feel like they fit in the classic era, they make sense, they're just a natural follow through, but they didn't exist there.

And then there's sometimes going out of our way to do something really different, and that's something like the Skyborne and Zephras, where we go to a part of the world we've never seen before, never even thought existed before so that we can tell all three types of stories and of all three types of content. That ensures that there's always room to add more things. If we only did what was expected, we would run out very quickly and we want to do the unexpected.

IGN: I imagine there's plenty of loose threads that you can pull at to find new content without having to go to outer space.

Zierhut: Correct, correct. Now, that said, the Dark Portal exists, Northrend exists, Pandaria exists, and we could make minor forays into those areas. We might have a dungeon or a quest that takes you there for a mission or two and come back.

Those [are] things that we're not doing soon, but it is something we think about within the scope of what we might do eventually with Forever. But the key detail there is Eastern Kingdoms and Kalimdor are your home. You don't have capital cities, you don't have auction houses and innkeepers and things like that outside of Eastern Kingdoms and Kalimdor. We won't introduce new capital cities in this plan. Okay. You always come home.

IGN: Speaking of which, housing. I know you have mentioned housing as a possibility for Forever, but I mean, I love housing in Midnight. It's one of my favorite things to do in my down time in between raids. Coming to Forever anytime soon?

Zierhut: It’s definitely something we’ve heard players ask about, and it’s a very interesting idea. That said, we don’t have any plans to add player housing to Forever right now.

IGN: So talking about the raids, I know that one of the guiding principles for endgame is this horizontal progression where it's not like a new raid comes out, that's the only place to get gear now. Can you tell me a little bit more about that? Is there going to be a point where there's seven different raids out and it's kind of expected to do all of them to get the best gear because they're all at the same level?

Zierhut: I think it's something we're definitely cognizant of. At some point there are too many raids and too many dungeons. We know we don't have to solve that yet, but we have lots of solutions that we're banding through like, okay, when we have too many, how do we curate it or control it so it's not overwhelming?

And so we're definitely keeping that idea in mind. We don't really have anything to talk about now other than we're aware of the issue, we're thinking about it, we have plans and ideas, they just haven't been fully explored. We're just too focused right now on shipping the game. But it's not a case of we're just going to ship it and figure it out later. We have really good ideas and plans, just can't talk about them yet.

As far as horizontal expansion of the game, there's lots of places where we are doing that. The legacy system is, I think, one of the big features there, where we're encouraging people to make new characters and experience the journey again. And that supports us saying, 'Hey, we're going to add a new level 30 zone or a new level 40 dungeon.' And the best way to experience those is to make a new character and level up to those levels and play it at that level. Don't just go in and crush it with a level 60 character. It won't be that much fun.

So definitely horizontal expansion is a big thing that we're interested in doing. Also in terms of itemization, I showed off at BlizzCon how we're doing a lot of trinkets that vary in power based on what kind of creature you're fighting or what kind of environment you're in. And we will be leaning into that, collecting different items that have different purposes and sort of a bag of tricks with your trinkets.

Now that said, we know that means there's going to be a burden on bag space eventually. Oh my God, I've got 50 different trinkets in my bag. So we will be taking care as the game grows, making sure there's enough storage for it all.

As it is right now, everybody has a bigger bank than they started with in the classic era, so they can store what we're giving them right now, but we'll be watching that storage problem. And again, trying to make as many different interesting items that are real choices about which one I should use is one of our itemization goals.

IGN: I think one of the things that follows from that is that you're also going to want different specs for those situations as well. I know that one of the problems that I've always had with Classic WoW, at least pre-Wrath of the Lich King, was respec costs. And that's something that has been solved in the modern version of the game. How flexible are people going to be with their talents or are people going to be stuck with their build and just relying on gear to handle different situations?

Zierhut: The first thing is that we have dual spec in the game at launch. So you'll be able to have two different specializations, so you can have two different builds available. Our experience is that most of the time in classic content, two builds is enough, but that's certainly something we would watch. Would we ever want to have a third spec, for example? I wouldn't take that off the table. We don't need it now, but I could imagine a future where that becomes something desirable.

What I think we don't want to do, just because it's a different game, is have you able to change your loadout on the fly talent by talent. It gets a little bit too overwhelming and finicky. The danger there is it becomes the expectation that for every encounter you're going to change your talents, and then that becomes not so approachable and familiar.

It starts to become a different game. So I think we do want to keep talents being a commitment. I can't just change them at any moment, but we do have ideas and plans for making it a little easier to change your talent spec when you need to change it. And of course, dual specs, you can have two different specs available to you at all times.

IGN: One of the things that I've been seeing covering the beta is a lot of griefing, and I know there was a controversy around character names as well. How are you going to maintain a friendly atmosphere so that people don't get to the point where they're so afraid of dealing with other people that they just shut themselves in and go solo?

Zierhut: Right. I agree with you, that's a problem in all of gaming, right? Yeah. It's one of the problems that gaming is desperately trying to solve. And our big answer to it is I think the healthiest answer, which is, it's our duty to make a game that pushes people towards positive social interactions and doesn't push people towards toxic social interactions.

And then if you can get enough positive interactions, you can turn the tide of where most people want to be nice, want to cooperate, and the jerks [are] in the minority. And so we're doing a lot of things to lean into what we call pro-social design. Again, the camping system is a good example of that. When I run into somebody out in the world, I'm happy to see them.

Having quests that require you to be in a group to complete the elite quests or group quests are another way where like, 'Hey, I wanted to be able to finish this quest line.' I can't just yell at the whole zone about they're all jerks. I need to be friends with people, more cross-linking in professions. Hey, I want to be able to craft this thing. I might need another person to help me craft it. I can't just go to the auction house and buy everything I need. Any other players to put down a work bench from a campsite or do an enchantment without a Vellum Scroll? So I got to be able to work with other people and do things. Dungeons and raids requiring groups.

One thing we're doing that's very different from later WoW expansions is we are having 10, 20 and 40 player raids as well as five player dungeons. we have four different types of endgame content sizes [for] endgame content people are playing in. And what that does is help people create more extended social networks.

A good illustration: If we go to the Barrow Deeps raid and we're going to go on Friday night, but our 10th player doesn't show up, we only have nine people, what do we do? Well, if all you have is 10 player raids, you might just be stuck or you might have to go to just shouting on LFG to see if somebody could join you. But if you also have a 20 and 40 player raid you do each week, you say, 'Hey, what about Jane from our 20 player raid that we did two nights ago? She was cool. Let's ask her and see if she can go to our 10 player raid with us.' So by having different sizes and different groups, you get a more resilient social network.

And the more resilient and positive the social network is, the less people are tempted to act out and act like jerks. That's sort of our belief, that people are fundamentally more interested in being good. We just have to lead them in that direction and have designs that encourage positive social interactions.

Other things in that space, we also have the ‘recently played with’ list. So when you've played with somebody, we show you the people you've recently played with so you can find them again. That could be people you traded with, people you grouped with, who you cast spells on. They all show up in that list. And then when we talk about how we place people out in the world, we have to distribute the population. If there's 5,000 people in Elwynn, they can't all be in the exact same version of Elwynn, they have to be in different ones.

Well, who gets put in which version of Elwyn at what time? We try to put people together in cohorts where they will keep seeing the same people over and over again. And we know that repeat social interactions encourage people to be kinder to each other.

We're mean to strangers and we're less mean to our neighbors and the person we see drive by or walk by with their dog every day because we'll see them again and we don't want to have a bad relationship with them. So seeing people multiple times over days and weeks also encourages us as human beings to be kinder to each other. So a lot of that type of design, if that makes sense.

IGN: Yeah, that sounds good. I know that it's kind of hard to just police people, especially when there's just so many people playing.

Zierhut: It can't be all punishment, all punishment. It's got to be sort of a positive inducement like, Because I was a nice person and played nice with others, this cool thing happened to me. You know what? Maybe I should be nice again tomorrow.

IGN: What is the Classic era, do you think?

Zierhut: I mean, there's different eras to different people. Some people will say it's only the original game because that's what they remember because they were playing it actively. They were 14 years old in 2004 and it was their whole world.

For some people it's going to be Burning Crusade or Wrath of the Lich King because that's when they played it. I've talked to people who the first time they played was Mists of Pandaria and that's it for them. So everybody has a different line on where it was. And even beyond that, people like, 'I started playing in Legion and I loved it. It was the best expansion ever.' There's people across the whole timeline that will have different opinions on that.

IGN: Yeah. I want to meet the people who are like, 'Shadowlands Classic is my thing.'

Zierhut: I'm sure that those people, they may not be noisy now, but give yourself five or six years and yeah, they'll come out of the woodwork, 'That was the best time ever. Trust me.' Once you get some distance, [the expansions] all have amazing things. It's when you're too close to appreciate what was great about them, but once there's distance, they're all amazing in different ways.

IGN: I know that a really cool story that I covered a couple weeks ago is the ‘Kyle's Gone Missing’ quest getting added into the game. And I loved that. Are there more things like that that were added to the game maybe a little bit later than Burning Crusade or Vanilla that are so iconic to World of Warcraft, regardless of whether or not they were in Classic?

Zierhut : Yeah. I think we've definitely talked about them. I think our only limitation has been time, how much time and bandwidth do we have to do it? So a really good example of that is, the area of Southern Dustwallow Marsh was redone post-Burning Crusade, and this little town called Mudsprocket, little goblin town got added to it. And we think it would be amazing to try to have our version of Mudsprocket and what was going on with the goblins in Southern Dustwallow and things like that. So there's a lot of things that happened during Burning Crusade, Wrath of the King, [and] Cataclysm that we like to make echoes and references to.

A good example of that we looked at earlier today with another journalist was in the zone of Shen’dralas, which is one of our smaller new zones. There's a character named Mordent Evenshade who is some kind of a highborn elf. Maybe he's actually a Skyborne elf. And he was introduced in Cataclysm as part of letting the Night Elves become mages, which was a big, big cultural break for Night Elves because magic was forbidden for them. And he shows up in Shen’dralas and he has his own story connected to the new stories we're telling. And so we like to have those kinds of echoes of what was going on, even if they're not exactly the same, of things that were done after the original classic era. They can still fit in our world.

IGN: When I think of Mount Hyjal, I think of the Cataclysm version of the zone and this (Forever version) looks completely different.

Zierhut: It's a very different experience without flying, because you have to walk along the ground and see it from that level. Whereas the Cataclysm version is fun. It's super fun, but you're moving from place to place, flying from these high points, and now you're down on the ground and you have to do the big walk up the mountain.

Cataclysm also had the Firelands section and we didn't make that big change. We have that whole additional area to work with that's not been taken over with lava, so there's more space to work with. So it'll have a very different feel.

I think one of the things I really like [about] Mount Hyjal is that as you walk through it, I'm like, Oh, I remember this spot. This spot is where I fought the demon Azgalor. Wait, that's Azgalor's skull on the ground there. There's these call-outs back to the Mount Hyjal raid that are super cool where you recognize the locations and buildings from when you saw it in a different era of the game. I think that's a lot of fun.

IGN: Are there more secret places that weren't added to the original game that were supposed to be? The Emerald Dream, I think was.

Zierhut: We'd love to explore the Emerald Dream at some point. So I think it's on our list of things we want to do. Grim Batol, we'd love to go to Grim Batol at some point. There was a dungeon in Cataclysm, but it was just a dungeon. We'd like to actually go explore the depths of Grim Batol and up to the tops of the towers and really see the whole place the way you saw Blackrock Mountain.

IGN: That place was wiped out by the time the classic era begins, right?

Zierhut: It's still there, but it's not clear what's been going on inside the mountain. The orcs have lost some control over it. There's cultists who come in later in Cataclysm. It's still there in Cataclysm.

It's just Cataclysm, there's a dungeon where you kind of fly... It's the one where you're on the flying dragons, you have kind of a bombing run before you land and do the full dungeon. We just like to go into it in more depth and fully explore it. Tim is showing on his screen a whole new dungeon that we've added. This is at the north end of Un’Goro Crater, and it's kind of a reference to some of the things that happened in Wrath of the Lich King where there were these titan sites on the north rim of Un’Goro.

Tim Jones: This an example of in Wrath of the Lich King, like you said, you could take a teleportation device from Sho’lazar Basin in Northrend to this location, the Shapers Terrace, which is north of Un’Goro. And so it is an example of, yes, there's definitely elements.

The Eastern Kingdoms and Kalimdor, that is our canvas. There are so many spaces and zones that never existed in Vanilla, places that we haven't really fully explored, like you said, the Emerald Dream. There's definitely places to explore in the Caverns of Time that we've never been to. The Riverglades, we went there a little bit earlier on our jaunt around the world, but that represents, just there was never a zone there and that space got destroyed in the cataclysm by Deathwing. But before then, what could it have been? And so we reached back into lore from Warcraft 1 and Warcraft 2.

There's a faction called the Brotherhood of the Horse. And so we craft this story with Chris Metzen helping us along the way to really figure out, okay, maybe this was an area where the the Alliance was chasing armies of the Horde out even further east than the Redridge Mountains, but they never got help from the Alliance, and so they had to settle on the frontier.

So there's opportunities like that to create brand new spaces and opportunities like this where it's like, yes, this was lightly touched on in a future expansion, but can we take that small little space and expand it into a dungeon, expand it into a zone, into a new raid? There's so many opportunities with the base world.

IGN: Is that going to be the shape of story additions that are coming to Forever? Things that were hinted at or referenced in other versions of the game or even the novels?

Jones: It's one of the pieces of the pie. Yeah.

Zierhut: It’s probably about a third of the pie. Probably about a third of it is things you expected, you've been waiting to see forever. And another third are things that just fit in the world and they always belong there.

And the last third are brand new things that you never imagined could be there. Another good example, we have all of the terrain for Gilneas is in the game. So Gilneas from Cataclysm, where the Worgen start, is in our world and we want to go there eventually and tell a new story in Gilneas. You can't go in there right now. Sharks will eat you. But when we do go to Gilneas, there will be a whole new story there and a chance to explore Gilneas before it gets destroyed in the Cataclysm. So lots of those kinds of opportunities.

Zierhut: Silvermoon we would like to get to eventually as well. Right now, Silvermoon's a big focus in Retail, so we think it's better for us to focus elsewhere, to not have overload on so much of the same story on every version.

Jones: But I think our attitude is [that] we are in a kind of a time bubble, right? We're locked in the place in between the end of Warcraft 3 and before Burning Crusade. And everything about Azeroth existed, even Outland exists, even Northrend exists, like Quel’Thelas exists. All these places are there. And I don't think if we ever went to Northrend, we wouldn't be visiting the version that you see in Wrath of the Lich King, but could we visit some extremely hostile level 60 version of it because Arthas is still in the stage where he's sending Kel’Thuzad to Eastern Kingdoms to assault Eastern Plaguelands? We could. There's so much that we can do with the timeline that we're in.

IGN: I do want to ask about the Skyborne and the reasoning behind adding them instead of some of the other races that existed in Azeroth already, like the Goblins or the Blood Elves.

Zierhut: We knew that we wanted to bring in more of the elves into the game. We know they're the most popular races in World of Warcraft historically. And in particular, the current alliance and Horde races from the Classic Era have the unfortunate feature that they tend to cause a faction imbalance. There's a certain... A lot of players who don't want to play a monster, to put it really honestly. They don't want to be an Orc or a Troll or a Tauren or Undead. They want to have something that looks prettier. It's not everybody.

And so we knew that having elves available on both sides would help with our faction balance, and it'd be very popular with the players. So then it became a question of, well, which elves do we want to tell a story of? There's lots of different elves in this world. Elves are one of the races that were all over Kalimdor and The Eastern Kingdoms in times past. So where do we want to go? Which elves should we tell a story about? And you mentioned Silvermoon, and this is a story that Retail had recently told, and we didn't want to get in each other's way of telling that story. We want to give them time to let their Silvermoon story breathe and do everything they wanted with it. And then once they were done with it, we could maybe then go visit Silvermoon.

So let's not do that. Let's not do more on the Night Elves. So who else do we have? Well, we have the elves from Dire Maul, the Shen’dralas elves, and what story could we tell from them? What happened to them? Some of them survived inside Dire Maul with Prince Tortheldrin, but where did the rest go? And that's where the idea for the Skyborne Elves came from. They're refugees from that civilization.

Jones: We are in Zephras Isle [now]. So if you look up into the sky, you can see elements of the

Jones: The Skywall architecture from the Elemental Plane of Air, because that is part of the story that as refugees, they allied with air elementals to create this kind of refugee island in the sky. And there's going to be exciting opportunities to explore more of their history in future patch content, [and] raid content. Al’Akir is definitely like... I mean, we fought Ragnaros and we fought Prince Thunderaan when folks were trying to craft Thunderfury back in Vanilla WoW. So dealing with these elemental deities has been part of WoW's history. And I think it's exciting that this race is connected so heavily to [those stories].

Zierhut: Yeah. So just exciting to keep telling these stories and the Skyborne are very deeply connected to the stories we plan to tell. This is not just sort of an island off in Skywall [where] we'll drop the story and never go anywhere. The Shen’dralar elves are connected to Shen’dralas, that new zone and connected to the Shen’dralar Elves in Dire Maul.

And we'll have more ongoing stories with Prince Tortheldrin and Dire Maul and what was really going on there, a story that Chris Metzin always had something in his mind, but we never got to tell that story. Now we get to go back and tell more of what was really happening around Dire Maul and how they got in the situation they were in.

IGN: So, obviously three different versions of World of Warcraft is a lot of game for anyone.

Zierhut: Yeah, but for different types of players or different types of gameplay they want, right?

IGN: Right. Do you imagine a world where the patch cadence is such that there's downtime in Retail so people pick up Forever and then downtime in Forever so people pick up Retail? Or do you think people are going to find their home among one of these three games and really embrace it?

Zierhut: I think there will definitely be downtime where you can play both games. In particular, just because the modern game is focused more on the sort of level 60 or max-level endgame progression rating, or PVP, arenas or battlegrounds. They're focused very much on that, and that tends to come in sort of bursts.

And then between those bursts, there's time to say, 'You know what? I'm just going to level up a new character in World of Warcraft Forever and learn a new tradeskill and earn some more legacy points and unlock that cool cosmetic in that game.' So there's opportunities for different types of gameplay in different games, and I think there will definitely be players who are playing both, and I think that's exciting and great.

Not sure which 3D printer to get? Read on below for a bit of detail on each deal.

The Bambu P2S and P1S are the best Bambu 3D printers for most people; these are Bambu's mid-range models and offer several useful premium features at a reasonable cost. The P2S is the second generation iteration and features a host of upgrades that will warrant its higher cost for some people.

Larger colorized 5" touchscreen display and more powerful processor

Hardened steel nozzles with 30 second nozzle swaps

Both the Bambu P2S and P1S are almost entirely fully assembled out of the box and setup should take under 15 minutes. Unlike cheaper 3D printers, these models feature a fully enclosed chamber, which is necessary to stabilize temperature and ambient conditions in order to produce more consistent results. They boast an acceleration speed of up to 20000 mm/s² and can print a benchy in 18 minutes. A built-in camera allows you to remotely monitor the printing process.

The Combo models include the Automatic Material System or AMS. This module basically allows for multi-filament printing, which means you can use up to four different types of filament material or colors per AMS (you can daisy chain up to four AMS to manage as many as 16 different filaments). The AMS itself normally retails $350, so it's best to get it in this combo, especially if you plan on getting it anyway in the long run.

The A1 Mini is Bambu's most affordable 3D printer. This is an excellent entry level printer for someone who's just starting out. Since this is a more compact design, the A1 Mini is ideal for smaller projects using PLA filament.

The main difference between the A1 and the A1 Mini is the build volume; the A1 has a larger working area. There are some other benefits to the A1's larger footprint like a larger touchscreen, but functionally the two are nearly identical. The A1 Combo model includes the Automatic Material System or AMS for multi-filament printing.

Bambu H2C, H2D, and H2S AMS Combo 3D Printers

If you're ready to graduate to the best of the best, then Bambu's H2 large-format printer series should be on your list of potential candidates. There are three variants in the series. The H2S is the most economical model and has a single nozzle. The H2D upgrades to a dual nozzle. The H2S is the flagship model with a multi-nozzle head that can fit up to seven nozzles, making it the best option for multi-color printing. Note that although the overall dimensions are the same, the H2S has the most build volume because the nozzle head is the smallest.
